# Changelog

Notable changes to the OpenCTEM API. Release notes for each version are
published at https://docs.openctem.io (operations/release-notes-*).

## Unreleased

Unreleased changes are kept one file per change in [`changelog.d/`](changelog.d/README.md) and folded in here at release.

## v0.11.0 and earlier

### Security: a delegated group manager changes only groups they fully cover

- Unassigning an asset from an access group, changing its ownership type and
  removing someone else from a group now need the caller to hold every asset
  the group holds (owners, admins and full-data roles are not capped; leaving
  a group oneself is always allowed). Before, a restricted manager (a BU lead
  with `groups:write`) could strip another BU's group of an asset or a member
  (RFC-050 W7). Adding members already had this cap (D13).

### Security: a restricted member cannot write asset-less exposures

- `POST /exposures`, `POST /exposures/ingest` and the bulk ingest refuse an
  exposure without `asset_id` from a member whose data scope is restricted
  (400 `asset_id is required`; a bulk item is reported and dropped). An
  asset-less exposure is in nobody's asset scope (owner decision D11), and the
  fingerprint upsert let a restricted member overwrite an existing asset-less
  exposure's severity, title and details, e.g. downgrade a critical one
  (RFC-050 W1). Administrators, full-data roles, sensors and
  internal jobs are unchanged; out-of-scope asset ids were already refused.

### Security: a ticket webhook can never close a finding

- **Jira and GitHub inbound sync only report work state**.
  A Jira webhook may move a finding to `confirmed`, `in_progress` or
  `fix_applied`, never to `resolved`, `false_positive`, `accepted` or
  `duplicate`: a webhook has no person who holds `findings:verify` or an
  approval. A ticketing integration whose `ticketing.status_inbound` maps a
  Jira status to a closing status is refused on save (400); such entries in
  stored configs are ignored, and the webhook checks the target again before
  applying it. The stock Jira "Duplicate" mapping was removed (marking a
  duplicate is a triage decision, `POST /findings/{id}/duplicates`).
- The tenant's own `status_inbound` overlay now applies to inbound webhooks
  (before, only the stock map did), within the same three statuses.
- Inbound status changes are recorded in the finding's history with the
  integration (`jira` / `github`) and the ticket as the actor.

### Security: the platform console answers only to private networks by default

- New `ADMIN_ALLOWED_CIDRS` (comma-separated CIDRs or addresses): every `/api/v1/admin` route, the console sign-in included, refuses other client networks with 403 `ADMIN_NETWORK_NOT_ALLOWED`. Default: loopback, RFC 1918 and IPv6 unique local addresses. The client address is the TCP peer or `X-Forwarded-For` from `SERVER_TRUSTED_PROXIES` only.
- A console sign-in from another address than the administrator's last one is audited (`console.new_network_sign_in`) and emailed to every administrator.
- A read-only administrator sees counts, not people: organization member lists return counts by role only, organizations show the owner count without emails, and the account search (Console > Users) needs ops_admin or above. Every member-list view is audited (`organization.users_view`).
- **Upgrade note:** an operator who reaches the console from a public address must set `ADMIN_ALLOWED_CIDRS` before upgrading, to their own address or network (for example `203.0.113.7/32`), or to `0.0.0.0/0,::/0` to keep it open to every network, or the console answers 403. Behind the gateway and the web console, keep them in `SERVER_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (the Compose stack does) so the API sees the real client address.

### Security: the platform administrators' audit log is append-only and hash-chained

- `admin_audit_logs` refuses updates, deletes and truncation (database triggers; the API role also loses its `UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`TRUNCATE` grants), and every row is linked into a SHA-256 chain computed by the database, so an edited or removed row is detectable. Migration 002545 chains the existing rows in the order they were written.
- Retention (`ADMIN_AUDIT_RETENTION_*`) now goes through `admin_audit_prune`: it removes only the oldest rows, never any newer than one year (a lower `ADMIN_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` acts as 365), and anchors the chain where it stopped.
- New: `GET /api/v1/admin/audit-logs/chain` (any administrator) and the Security > Activity banner show whether every entry verifies; `bootstrap-admin verify-audit [-json]` (admin-cli image) does the same from the command line and exits 1 on a break.
- Deleting an administrator no longer clears `admin_id` on their audit rows (the foreign key is dropped).
- **Upgrade note:** nothing to run: the migration revokes the grants itself, and the `db-roles` bootstrap keeps them revoked. Tooling that deleted rows from `admin_audit_logs` directly must use `SELECT admin_audit_prune(cutoff, max_rows)` instead.

### Security: the platform administrators' audit log can be streamed off the box

- New `ADMIN_AUDIT_SINK`: every administrators' audit row is sent, as written, with its hash-chain position and hash (not the request body), and the chain head every `ADMIN_AUDIT_SINK_HEAD_INTERVAL` (default 15 minutes). Destinations: `https://…` (JSON per POST, signed with `ADMIN_AUDIT_SINK_SECRET`), `syslog+tls://` (RFC 5424, optional mutual TLS) or `file:///path` (JSON lines). Someone who controls the database can no longer re-sign the chain without the copy already sent disagreeing.
- Delivery never slows the console (queued, in order, retried; a full queue drops the newest event with an error line). A batch that does not continue the last delivered row is still sent, flagged with a `gap` field, counted and logged. A destination that cannot be used stops the API's start-up.
- **Upgrade note:** optional; nothing changes unless `ADMIN_AUDIT_SINK` is set. For a SaaS deployment, point it at the SIEM.

### Security: the admin console sign-in is no longer a password oracle

- A correct tenant password of an account that is not an administrator, or of an
  inactive or locked administrator, now answers the same 401 as a wrong
  password (the real reason stays in the audit record).
- A correct password no longer resets the account's failed-sign-in counter until
  the account is confirmed an active, unlocked administrator, and a sign-in
  refused because the identity provider is required counts as a failure toward
  the lockout instead of clearing it.
- The console `/login` counts failures per client address and asks for the
  CAPTCHA after repeated failures, like the tenant sign-in.

### Security: owner recovery needs a reason and a fresh authenticator code

- `POST /api/v1/admin/tenants/{tenantId}/users` with `"recovery": true` (super admin, every owner suspended) now also requires `reason` (10 to 500 characters, kept in the admin audit log) and `totp_code`, a fresh code from the console authenticator. Without them it answers 400 or 401 `STEP_UP_REQUIRED`, and nothing is created.
- **Upgrade note:** scripts that call owner recovery must send both fields.

### Security: the platform console has its own site, private networks only

- The gateway serves the platform console on its own site: `https://<host>:8443` by default (`OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=port`) or its own DNS name (`OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=host`, `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_HOST`). Only `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_ALLOWED_CIDRS` (default: loopback, RFC 1918, IPv6 ULA) gets past it; others get 403.
- The main site answers 404 for `/admin` and `/api/v1/admin`. The web console (`OPENCTEM_ADMIN_PLANE=separate`) serves only the console on the console site and never on the main one; it reaches the API's console listener (`ADMIN_API_URL`, `ADMIN_LISTEN_ADDR=:8081`).
- The Compose kit turns all of this on; `setup.sh` takes `--admin-site port|host|off`, `--admin-host <name>`, `--admin-port <port>`, `--admin-cidrs "<cidrs>"` and `--admin-public`, and prints the console URL and an SSH-tunnel line.
- **Upgrade note:** the console moves from `https://<host>/admin` to `https://<host>:8443/admin` (or your `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_HOST`), reachable only from private networks unless you set `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_ALLOWED_CIDRS`. Publish port 8443 (the Compose file does), or set `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=host` with a DNS name that points at the gateway. Administrators sign in again there. Keep the old layout with `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=off`, `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_PLANE=shared` and no `ADMIN_LISTEN_ADDR` (not recommended).

### Security: no console secret is readable in a cookie

- The platform console's CSRF token cookie `admin_csrf` is HttpOnly and scoped to `/api/v1/admin`, like the session cookie. The console receives the token in the body of the responses that open a session (the TOTP step, the identity-provider callback) and of `GET /api/v1/admin/auth/validate` (`csrf_token`), keeps it in memory and echoes it in `X-CSRF-Token`. No readable copy is set; the old JS-readable `admin_csrf` at `/` is cleared on sign-in and sign-out. A script on a tenant page, including one on the same host when the console is on a port of its own, cannot read the console's token.
- **Upgrade note:** administrators signed in to the console when this ships are asked to sign in to the console again the next time they open it.

### Security: console identity and trust changes need a fresh authenticator code

- Every platform-console write that changes an identity, a privilege, an organization's trust or a platform setting asks for a fresh authenticator code (step-up), or rides the five-minute step-up window of the same console session: administrators (provision, change, delete, reset, break-glass test, identity-provider unbind, ending a session), the platform identity provider, account support actions on users, organization creation, access-request approval, owners, organization SSO, module grants, scan-approval policies, the audit-chain rebaseline, and the sign-up, e-mail, legal, limits, modules, platform-sensor-proof, content-pack and program-feed settings. A stolen console session alone can no longer add an administrator or swap the console's identity provider. The routine writes left (limits, idle exemption, rejecting a request, announcements, feed sync, AI-client blocks, target mappings, the e-mail test) are listed with their reason, and CI fails on an unclassified console write.
- The API answers `401 ADMIN_STEP_UP_REQUIRED` without a code (header `X-Admin-Step-Up`); the console asks for it and retries. Forms that already asked for a code (`totp_code`) send it in that header as well, so nobody is asked twice.
- Migration 002472 adds `admin_sessions.step_up_at` (nullable, no backfill).
- **Upgrade note:** an administrator who signs in only through the platform identity provider has no console authenticator and gets `403 STEP_UP_UNAVAILABLE` on these actions; keep at least one super admin with a console authenticator (every break-glass account has one).

### Security: the all-in-one image no longer exposes the platform console without the gateway

- With `GATEWAY=off` the console used to listen on `0.0.0.0:3001` without
  forwarding the client address, so the API's admin network check saw
  `127.0.0.1` and allowed every caller. The console now always binds to
  `127.0.0.1` and, with `GATEWAY=off`, is not started unless
  `OPENCTEM_CONSOLE_STANDALONE=true`. Port 3001 is no longer part of the
  published-ports guidance.

### Security: the sign-in routes refuse writes a browser sends for another site

- `POST /api/v1/auth/register`, `/login`, `/mfa/verify`, `/mfa/enroll/*`,
  `/token`, `/refresh`, `/verify-email`, `/forgot-password`,
  `/reset-password`, `/create-first-team`, `/discover`, the OAuth and SSO
  callbacks, and the console's `/api/v1/admin/auth/session`, `/mfa`,
  `/logout`, `/idp/start` and `/idp/callback` answer 403 when the browser
  says the request comes from another site: an `Origin` that is neither the
  request's host nor in `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`, `Origin: null`, or no
  `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` other than `same-origin`/`none`. These routes
  run before a session exists and set session cookies, so without the check a
  page on another site could sign a visitor into the attacker's account
  (login CSRF) where the API is reachable from browsers directly.
- Calls that send neither header (the web console's server, scripts, CI) are
  not affected. Rejections count in `csrf_rejections_total{reason="cross_site"}`.

### Security: the API reference is not public in production

- With `APP_ENV=production` the API no longer serves the interactive reference at `/docs`, and `/openapi.yaml` needs a signed-in user. The public reference lives on docs.openctem.io.
- Platform administrators read both through the console session at `/api/v1/admin/docs` and `/api/v1/admin/openapi.yaml`, in every environment.
- Outside production `/docs` and `/openapi.yaml` stay public for development.
- The reference page now loads one version-pinned script with a subresource integrity hash and no longer builds URLs from the request's `Host` header.
- **Upgrade note:** links to `https://<your-host>/docs` stop working in production; use the documentation site or the console route.

### Security: approval requests made by an actor need one more sign-off; the security pool is harder to stack

- A request a linked ticket, VEX or AI triage makes (no person behind it) needs one sign-off more than its tier asks, so the person who moved the ticket cannot complete it with one account. A ticket's proposed acceptance end is within the organization's cap for the finding.
- A member of the security pool group counts as the pool only 24 hours after joining it, and adding or removing a member of that group (or deleting it) needs a recent re-authentication.

### Security: sensors no longer set an asset's owner or data classification

- A sensor report is always a scan source, whatever it claims, and scanners are not trusted for criticality, owner or data classification by default. Ingest no longer fills `owner_ref` or `data_classification` on existing assets, and an asset a sensor creates does not take them. An organization can trust scanners for an attribute in its settings.

### Security: asset group counts follow the reader data scope

- The asset group list, a group, the group stats and the group returned after a change now count only the assets the reader may see: asset count, per-kind counts, risk score and finding count. A member restricted to some assets used to see tenant-wide numbers (L-18), and could probe them with the risk and has-findings filters. Owners, administrators and full-data roles see the whole group as before.

### Security: `GET /api/v1/assets/stats?count_by=` is capped

- `count_by` accepts only property keys of the schema (a synonym counts as its key), at most 10. Each field was one more GROUP BY over the caller's assets, and the list was unbounded.

### Security: asset references are tenant-checked in the database (migrations 000920-000922)

- Every table that stores an asset id next to a `tenant_id` (27 columns:
  findings, exposures, exposure events, pipeline runs, scan sessions,
  suppressions, SLA policies, scope rows, grants, relationships, ...) gets a
  composite foreign key `(tenant_id, asset) → assets(tenant_id, id)`: a row of
  one organization can no longer point at another organization's asset,
  whatever writes it. Backstop for the application checks on `POST /findings`,
  exposure create/ingest and pipeline runs.
- **Deploy note:** `000921` first counts existing cross-tenant references and
  refuses to run, changing nothing, if there are any. See
  `docs/deployment/safe-deploy-and-migrations.md` ("Asset tenant foreign keys")
  for the listing query and the recovery steps. `000920` builds an index
  `CONCURRENTLY`; `000922` validates without blocking writes.

### Security: asset services list and create check the caller's data scope in the handler

- `GET` and `POST /api/v1/assets/{id}/services` now check that the asset is inside the caller's data scope in the handler itself and answer 404 when it is not, as the by-id service routes already did. The route-level data-scope guard already refused these requests; the handler check keeps them safe wherever the routes are mounted.
- New tests walk every registered `/api/v1/assets/{id}/...` route as a data-scoped member against an out-of-scope asset and require 404, so a sub-resource route mounted without the guard fails CI.

### Security: evidence images lose their metadata; optional malware scanning marks flagged files

- Uploaded PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP files are stored without their metadata
  (EXIF with GPS, XMP, IPTC, comments, text chunks); pixels, color profile,
  transparency, animation and JPEG orientation are kept. The upload audit
  event records `original_sha256` and `metadata_removed`.
- Images above 50 megapixels are refused with `400 IMAGE_TOO_LARGE`
  (decompression bombs); damaged images with `400 IMAGE_INVALID`.
- New `STORAGE_CLAMD_ADDRESS` (off by default) scans new uploads with a
  ClamAV daemon. Flagged files are kept and marked (`scan_status`,
  `scan_result` in the attachment list), audited
  `attachment.malware_detected`, never embedded in reports, and download
  only with `?confirm=malware` (audited `attachment.infected_downloaded`);
  the console lists them apart and asks first. Examples:
  `api/deploy/docker-compose.clamav.yml`, `api/deploy/kubernetes/clamav.yaml`.
- Migration `002061_attachment_malware_scan` adds `attachments.scan_status`,
  `scan_result`, `scanned_at` (constant defaults, no rewrite) and a partial
  index.
- **Behaviour change:** an upload whose bytes start like an image but do not
  parse as one is now refused (`IMAGE_INVALID`) instead of stored.

### Security: attack simulations only target assets the member may act on

- Creating, updating and running an attack simulation now applies the scan
  act-scope rule to its target assets: an asset-id target must be a live
  asset of the organization that the acting member may act on, and a
  free-text target goes through the act-scope check. Anything else answers
  404. A run is re-checked, so a saved simulation stops running for a member
  who lost the asset. Before, any member with `validation:write` could point
  a live safe-check probe at an out-of-scope or another tenant's asset
  (RFC-050 W3).

### Security: public sign-in endpoints no longer reveal organizations or accounts

- `GET /auth/sso/providers?org=` answers an unknown organization with
  `{"providers":[]}` (200), like an organization without SSO; before it was a
  404 "Organization not found". `GET /auth/sso/{provider}/authorize` answers an
  unknown organization like a missing provider (404 "SSO provider not
  configured"). `GET /auth/saml/{org}/metadata` serves the SP metadata for any
  well-formed slug.
- `POST /auth/register` answers a new and an already registered email with the
  same body: it no longer returns the account id, states the same
  verification rule for both, checks the password policy before the account
  lookup (a weak password was refused only for a new email), and sends the
  verification email after the response.
- `POST /auth/forgot-password` does the lookup, the token write and the email
  after the response, so its latency does not depend on the account existing.

### Security: registration logs no longer carry the e-mail address

The "user registered" log line records the user id only. The e-mail address was written to the log unescaped (a log-injection vector) and is personal data that logs should not keep.

### Security: counts follow the reader's data scope, expired team memberships stop granting scope, and scope-rule delete is capped

- `asset_count` on access groups, the business unit rollup counters, `/scoping/summary` asset counts, `/attack-surface/stats` breakdown and average risk, and the exposure-chain summary now count only the assets the caller can see. Organization-wide configuration totals are unchanged and listed in the authorization matrix.
- A team membership past its end date no longer grants asset scope while waiting for the expiry controller (migration `002903`; it rebuilds the scope rows once).
- A caller limited to their scope can delete a scope rule only when every asset of its team and of the rule is in their scope. Deleting a rule rebuilds the scope rows of that organization only, not every organization's.

### Security: asset scope is enforced on compensating controls, business services and team activation

- A compensating control can only be linked to assets and findings the caller can see; updating, deleting or testing a control, and updating or deleting a business service, need every linked asset in the caller's data scope. A business service's `asset_count` counts only in-scope links.
- An API key with no user no longer reads every asset of the tenant: authentication refuses it and the data scope resolves to no rows. Migration `002895` revokes the remaining user-less keys. **Upgrade note:** mint a new key (it is bound to its creator) to replace any revoked organization key.
- `PUT /groups/{id}` with `is_active` applies the group scope cap and the security pool step-up. Switching a team on re-grants its bound roles, so it now passes the binding ceiling, the owner and step-up rule for privileged roles, and the self-membership rule. Switching a team off or deleting it drops its members' cached permissions at once.

### Security: automations cannot trigger each other in a loop

- An event caused by an automation step (a status change it made, the end of a
  scan it started) never starts the automation that caused it. It starts other
  automations only when they allow it with
  `trigger_config.allow_automation_triggers: true` (off by default), never past a
  chain depth of 3, and at most once per finding in 10 minutes. AI-triage events
  have the same cooldown.
- **Behaviour change:** an automation that ran on status changes made by another
  automation no longer does, unless it sets `allow_automation_triggers`.

### Security: automation runs act as one person, checked before every step

- A manual run (`POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/runs`) acts as the caller. It names
  its subject with `finding_id` or `asset_id`; `trigger_data` and trigger types
  other than `manual` are refused. The caller needs the permission of every step
  and the subject in their data scope. Before, any holder of
  `findings:workflows:write` could make an administrator's automation change any
  finding by naming it in `trigger_data`.
- An event run acts as the automation's owner (`created_by`). Creating, switching
  on, or changing what an automation does makes the editor its owner. Before each
  action and notification step the owner is checked live (active member,
  the step's permission, the subject in their data scope); a refused step fails
  with `AUTOMATION_RUN_NOT_AUTHORIZED` and changes nothing.
- Adding or removing an edge, deleting or editing a node, and switching an
  automation on need the permission of every step, like adding one. Notification
  steps need `integrations:read`; outbound HTTP needs `integrations:manage`.
- The `http_request` action is retired (outbound calls go through a notification
  integration): new nodes are refused, a stored one no longer runs (its step
  fails), its header values are no longer returned by the API, and response
  bodies and headers are no longer stored with the run. Building one needed
  `integrations:manage`.
- **Upgrade note:** an active automation with no owner (`created_by` empty) runs
  no step until someone with the needed permissions saves or switches it on again.

### Security: profile pictures load only from known avatar hosts

- A profile picture is shown to teammates, so an arbitrary URL could act as a tracking pixel and log their IP addresses and browsers. `PUT /api/v1/users/me` now refuses an `avatar_url` that is not an https URL (no credentials, no port) on a known avatar host: GitHub, Google, Gravatar or GitLab.com (400). An empty value still clears the picture.
- A picture from an identity provider on another host is dropped at account creation (the person shows initials); the sign-in is not affected.
- The web shows a stored picture only when it meets the same rule, so values saved before this change stop loading; commit-author pictures in the repository view follow the same rule.

### Security: every upstream response read is bounded

- SCM clients (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps), the Jira and
  DefectDojo clients, OAuth/SSO token and user-info calls, the LLM providers
  and S3 template downloads read upstream bodies without a size limit, so one
  hostile or broken endpoint could exhaust the API's memory (RFC-049 F-12).
  They now read through `httpsec.ReadLimited` / `httpsec.DecodeJSON` (10 MiB
  for API responses, the existing limits elsewhere).
- Reads that were capped with a plain `io.LimitReader` (Jira, OIDC token
  exchange, the CTEM-ID feed, the EPSS and KEV feeds, SBOM import) truncated
  silently; an oversize body is now an error, so a cut-off EPSS CSV no longer
  imports a partial score set. Finding report imports and attachments are
  capped on the read as well as on the declared size.
- security-lint Rule 8 fails CI on `io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` or
  `json.NewDecoder(resp.Body)` in the API.

### Security: bug-bounty program targets never reach platform sensors

- A target that only program entries cover is never sent to platform sensors, in every `SCOPE_ACTIVE_PROOF` mode: an explicit `sensor_preference: platform` answers `400 PLATFORM_SENSOR_REFUSED`, `auto` keeps the job on the organization sensors, and `POST /scope/check` answers the refusal code `program_platform`.
- A program out-of-scope item (and the unlisted apex of a program wildcard) stops every program entry of the organization from covering the name; the organization own entries are not affected.

### Security: restricted members no longer see campaign details outside their data scope

- A member restricted by data scope reaches only the remediation campaigns that touch their scope (one of its findings or its asset is in scope) or that they created. Any other campaign answers 404 to every read and write (get, findings, update, status, resolve, refresh, create-ticket, delete) and is not listed; the list total counts only visible campaigns.
- A member restricted by data scope reading a remediation campaign (`GET /api/v1/remediation/campaigns` and `/{id}`) no longer sees the explicit finding ids or the asset id of its filter that are outside their scope, nor the organization-wide risk fields. Counts were already scoped.
- The remediation key side table is joined to findings of the same tenant only (defence in depth).

### Security: a campaign's finding filter can no longer widen to the whole organization

- A campaign's `finding_filter` is parsed strictly: an unknown key, a value of
  the wrong type or a value that does not parse is refused with 400 on create
  and update. Before, such a condition was dropped:
  `{"asset_id":"bad","severity":"critical"}` covered, and resolved, every
  critical finding of the organization.
- A status alone (`{"statuses":["new"]}`) is no longer scope: such a campaign
  tracks nothing and cannot resolve. A stored filter that no longer parses
  tracks nothing and its resolve answers 400 until the scope is edited.
- `POST /api/v1/remediation/campaigns/{id}/resolve` now needs
  `findings:fix_apply` as well as `findings:remediation:write`, and works only
  on an `active` or `validating` campaign.

### Security: a campaign needs a real scope before it counts or resolves

- A campaign's scope must name what is fixed: an asset, CVEs, linked
  findings, a tool or a fix key. A filter of only severities, sources,
  statuses or search text ("every critical finding") now tracks nothing and
  its resolve answers 400, instead of acting on the whole organization.
- Upgrade: the migration lists, in its output, every open campaign that will
  track nothing (`campaign scope: tenant … campaign … (name) …` and a total).
  To check before upgrading, read only:
  `SELECT tenant_id, id, name FROM remediation_campaigns WHERE status NOT IN ('completed','canceled') AND finding_filter <> '{}'::jsonb AND NOT (finding_filter ?| ARRAY['asset_id','cve_ids','cve_id','finding_ids','finding_id','tool_name','remediation_key'])`.
  Give each one an asset, CVEs, findings or a tool.

### Security: changing a campaign needs every one of its findings in your scope

- A member restricted by data scope could update, pause, delete, refresh or
  open a Jira epic for a campaign shared with another team as soon as one of
  its findings was theirs. Those changes now need every finding of the
  campaign (and its asset) in their scope, or an empty campaign they created;
  otherwise they answer 403. Seeing the campaign still needs only one finding
  in scope, and resolve still changes only their own findings.
- A restricted member's new or changed campaign scope (`finding_filter`) must
  be theirs too: creating a campaign over, or re-scoping one onto, another
  team's findings, assets or CVEs answers 403 and saves nothing.
- The restricted campaign list examines every campaign of the organization
  instead of the first 1,000, so later campaigns are no longer missing.

### Security: a CAPTCHA protects self-service sign-up and request access

- With `CAPTCHA_TURNSTILE_SECRET` and `CAPTCHA_TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY` set,
  `POST /auth/register` requires a passing Cloudflare Turnstile token
  (`captcha_token`). It is checked before the account lookup, the same way for
  every address, and answers 400 `CAPTCHA_FAILED` otherwise. Request access
  already checked it.
- The register and request-access forms now render the check. Before, no form
  did, so setting the secret refused every request-access submission and
  registration had no CAPTCHA at all. Sign-up bots could create accounts and
  send verification emails from the platform's domain to any address.
- The server refuses to start with only one of the two variables. The web CSP
  allows frames from `https://challenges.cloudflare.com` only.

### Security: a CI break-glass override covers exactly one commit

- A gate override now needs the full commit id (40 or 64 hex characters) and
  matches only that commit. Before, an abbreviated id (7 characters or more)
  was matched as a prefix, so it also covered any other commit made to share
  the prefix (about 2^28 attempts for 7 characters).
- An override saved with an abbreviated id before this change no longer
  applies; create it again with the full id (overrides last at most 7 days).

### Security: CI tables keep no email and reference their tenant's rows only

- `ci_gate_overrides.created_by_email` is dropped: the break-glass creator is its user id, and the email is read from the user when the override is shown. The gate verdict, which CI jobs print in their logs, no longer names the person who created the break-glass.
- `ci_runs` and `ci_pipelines` reference their trust configuration with the tenant (composite foreign keys): a row can never point at another organization's configuration. Deleting a configuration still keeps its runs and pipelines as history.

### Security: the CI token exchange is limited per organization and issuer, not per address alone

- `POST /api/v1/ci/oidc/exchange` used one budget of 60 a minute per client address. Hosted CI runners share egress addresses across customers, so one busy pipeline fleet, or an attacker running jobs on the same runners, could throttle every other organization's CI.
- The exchange now counts 60 a minute per organization + token issuer at one address, under a per-address backstop of 600 a minute, both shared by every API replica. The issuer is read from the token without checking its signature, only to choose the bucket; the address stays in the key so junk tokens naming an organization from elsewhere cannot use up its budget.

### Security: a CI run's first verdict is final

- `POST /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}/evaluate` on a run that already has a verdict
  returns the stored verdict unchanged and records nothing. Before, a job could
  evaluate again (for example with `scan_failures: 0`) and overwrite a failing
  verdict, which dashboards, pipeline status and alerts read. A re-run of the
  pipeline gets its own run, as before.

### Security: CI fork events never stand for the default branch; GitHub App webhook replays and token scope

- A CI run triggered by a fork event (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`,
  a GitLab external pull request) carries the base branch's ref and commit.
  It was counted as a default-branch run: its findings became default-branch
  exposure and its verdict was posted as the "OpenCTEM gate" check on the
  base commit. Such a run is now never a default-branch run, its findings go
  to a `fork/...` branch that does not count as exposure (branch-only until a
  real branch sees them), and no check goes on the base commit.
- The GitHub App webhook refuses a replayed delivery: after the signature
  check each `X-GitHub-Delivery` id is accepted once for 24 hours across
  replicas, and the webhook fails closed (503) when the store is down.
- Installation tokens used to post checks and comments are narrowed to the
  one repository and to `checks: write`, `pull_requests: write`,
  `metadata: read`, and cached per repository.

### Security: a failed default-branch CI run can no longer become its own gate baseline

- A default-branch run was compared with what earlier runs had seen, so running a failed run again (or pushing
  again) turned every finding into "already on the default branch" and passed the gate. A default-branch run is
  now judged against the repository's **gate baseline** only.
- The first verified default-branch run of a repository records its baseline (the findings open on the default
  branch) and passes on them, once per repository; the verdict and the audit log say so. Secrets still block.
- New: `GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/ci/gate-baselines/{id}`. Recording a new baseline by hand needs
  `scans:ci:policy` and a recent sign-in, is audited at high severity and announced to administrators; removing it
  makes every finding count as new again and no run records another. Once a repository has a baseline, a pull
  request into the default branch treats a finding as pre-existing only if it is also in the baseline. Migration
  `ci_gate_baselines`.
- **Upgrade note:** the next verified default-branch run of each repository records its baseline.

### Security: a second pipeline on a commit cannot turn a failing "OpenCTEM gate" check green

- The GitHub check and the GitLab commit status of a commit now take the
  strictest of the latest verdicts of every pipeline on that commit. Before,
  each run posted its own verdict under the same name, and the code host
  keeps the latest one: a second workflow added by the pull request, or any
  later passing run of another pipeline, replaced a failing check. A re-run
  of the same pipeline still replaces its own earlier verdict.
- The GitHub App guide and the console tell administrators to set the
  required check's expected source to the OpenCTEM app, so a workflow's own
  token cannot post a check with the same name.

### Security: the CI gate fails a run that skips an expected scan

- A repository with a coverage expectation must report every expected capability (sast, sca, secrets, iac; an empty expectation means all four) in each CI run. A run that reports no tool for one gets the blocking reason `missing_capability` ("Expected scan missing"). Before, a pull request that edited its pipeline to drop a scanner passed on silence.
- A repository without an expectation is unchanged. Tool labels are self-declared: this closes the "report nothing" path, and it does not prove that a scan ran.

### Security: a CI run over the 100,000-finding cap fails its gate instead of judging a prefix

- A CI run records at most 100,000 findings for its gate. A run that reported more used to be judged on the
  first 100,000 only, so a blocking finding past the cap was missed and the run could pass. It now fails with
  the reason `too_many_findings` ("Too many findings to judge" on the CI/CD page), and the findings are still
  stored on the platform. Repeating sightings the run already recorded does not count as overflow.
- Migration `002140_ci_run_findings_over_cap` adds `ci_runs.findings_over_cap` (boolean, default false; no
  table rewrite).

### Security: the CI gate honors a suppression only while its rule applies

- A finding passed the CI gate as suppressed whenever any suppression link
  existed for it. The expiry job reopens a finding when its rule expires but
  keeps the link row, and links can name rules that are pending or rejected,
  so an expired or never-approved suppression let a finding pass every later
  pipeline. The gate now counts a suppression only through an approved,
  unexpired rule of the run's own organization (RFC-051 section 6).

### Security: CI gate policies honour data scope, and loosening one needs step-up

- **Data scope on gate policies.** A repository policy is listed, created,
  changed and deleted only for a repository in the caller's data scope (404
  otherwise); before, every `scans:ci:read` holder saw every repository
  policy and every `scans:ci:write` holder could change the gate of any
  repository. Organization and business unit policies are changed only by a
  caller with an unrestricted data scope (403).
- **Loosening the gate needs step-up and is announced.** A policy change
  that lets more findings pass (warn mode, a higher severity threshold,
  new-findings-only, KEV off, a weaker EPSS threshold or mode, or disabling
  or deleting a stricter policy) asks for a recent sign-in like a
  break-glass, is audited at high severity (`ci_gate_policy.loosened`) and
  notifies every owner and administrator on the `ci.break_glass` event. It
  used to bypass break-glass entirely: one policy change disabled the gate
  for every commit. Tightening is unchanged.

### Security: the CI gate fails when the job reports a capability that did not reach the platform

- The CI runner (openctemio/ci v0.4) sends each capability's state with the verdict request. The gate now reads
  it: a capability that failed, uploaded only partial results, was not uploaded or is missing fails the run
  with `capability_failed` ("Scan did not reach the platform"), naming the capability, its tool and the reason,
  even when the job's `scan_failures` count is zero. Unknown states count as not clean. Older runners that send
  no states are judged as before.

### Security: GitLab connections accept only group or project access tokens

- Connecting a GitLab group for CI statuses and merge request notes now checks that the token acts as a bot user (`GET /user` reports `bot: true`, the user of a group or project access token) and that this user is the token's own. Before, any direct member's personal access token with the `api` scope was accepted, so the gate was posted as that person and kept working with their access after they left the group.
- A connection made with a personal token before this change keeps working until it is removed. Reconnect the group with a group access token.

### Security: CI trust pins each organization's immutable id

- A GitHub or GitLab trust configuration matches organizations by name. The
  first admitted exchange now pins the name to its immutable id (GitHub
  `repository_owner_id`, GitLab `namespace_id`; table `ci_trust_owner_pins`,
  migration `ci_trust_owner_pins`, audited). A later token with the same name
  and another id (an organization renamed or deleted and its name registered
  by someone else) is refused and audited (`owner_id_mismatch`). Changing the
  configuration's issuer, owners or repositories drops its pins, which are
  taken again at the next run; `GET /api/v1/ci/trust-configs/{id}` lists them
  (`owner_pins`).

### Security: withdrawn CI trust takes effect at once

- Disabling or deleting a CI trust configuration, or changing its issuer or audience, revokes its pipelines and invalidates the upload tokens of its runs still running (audited, `ci_pipeline.revoked`). Before, those tokens kept working until they expired.
- A CI token without a numeric repository or project id, or without a usable workflow path, is refused. GitLab's `user_email` claim is never read or stored.

### Security: GitHub CI trust can require protected refs through deployment environments

- A CI trust configuration's **Protected branches and tags only** switch now works on GitHub: GitHub tokens carry no protected-ref claim, so the job must run in one of the configuration's listed deployment environments (whose deployment branch rules admit only protected refs). Before, a GitHub configuration with the switch silently admitted nothing.
- Saving a GitHub configuration with the switch and no environments is refused with a validation error.
- New tests pin the run token's least privilege over the real route registration (a run token reaches no tenant, console, API-key or MCP route; run routes accept no other credential) and the workload token's one-minute clock-skew bound.

### Security: GitHub pull request results are recorded on the pull request, never on a real branch

- A GitHub pull request run recorded its findings on its head branch's name. A pull request from a branch named
  like a real one (a fork's `main` in a private repository that sends tokens to fork pull requests, or
  `release/1.x` into `main`) wrote its findings into that real branch, which later pull requests are compared
  with: a later pull request with the same finding passed as "pre-existing". Results now go to `pull/<n>`, as
  the other providers already did (GitLab keeps `merge-requests/<n>`); every pull or merge request upload is
  forced onto its own scope whatever branch name a stored run carries.
- Existing branch rows and occurrences are not moved.

### Security: a CI repository name stays with the repository that first reported under it

- CI trust rules match GitHub and GitLab owners and repositories by name. A
  name can change hands: an organization or group renamed or deleted and its
  name registered by someone else, or a repository deleted and created anew.
  The exchange now binds a repository name to the immutable repository id
  that first reported under it (GitHub `repository_id`, GitLab `project_id`;
  Bitbucket already did this), so a different repository under the same name
  cannot report into the repository asset. It is refused and audited
  (`ci_run.token_refused`, rule `repository_binding`) until an administrator
  retires the old pipeline. A rename keeps the id and is admitted.

### Security: organizations can require OIDC for CI; on by default for new ones

- New setting **Require OIDC for CI** (`GET/PUT /api/v1/ci/settings`, `scans:ci:read` / `scans:ci:write`; console: top of Settings > Scanning > CI pipelines). When on, the key of a one-shot (CI) sensor is refused on every sensor route (protocol v2: `403` problem `ci-oidc-required`) and the refusal is audited (`ci_run.runner_key_refused`, at most once per sensor every ten minutes). CI jobs then authenticate only with their provider's OIDC token.
- Migration `001120` adds `tenants.ci_require_oidc`: existing organizations keep accepting CI sensor keys (`false`) and see a banner until they opt in; every organization created afterwards starts with it on.
- **Upgrade note:** after moving pipelines to OIDC, turn the setting on; a CI job that still sends a sensor key gets `403` once it is on.

### Security: per-run report cap and per-pipeline run rate for CI

- A CI run accepts at most 200 reports; one more answers `409`.
- A CI pipeline may start at most 300 runs an hour; beyond that the token exchange is refused and audited (`ci_run.token_refused`, reason `pipeline_rate`). Other pipelines of the repository are not affected.
- A test now pins that a secret a CI run uploads unmasked (as its value or in the snippet) is stored nowhere in clear, and never reaches the audit log.

### Security: re-running only the CI gate job can no longer pass on an empty run

- A retry or re-run of a pipeline's gate job opened a new aggregate run with no reports, which judged nothing and
  passed; the commit check took that latest verdict. Every job, retry and re-run attempt of one pipeline run
  (pipeline, provider run id, commit) now reports into one run: a later attempt re-opens it and the verdict covers
  every attempt's reports with today's decisions, so an approved exception or a fixed flaky scan can turn it green
  without a new commit.
- A re-opened run keeps its last verdict for the commit check and the merged-without-a-passing-gate check until it
  is judged again, so retrying one job of a failed pipeline cannot hide its failure.
- A capability that failed in an earlier attempt keeps failing the run until a report of that capability arrives;
  a runner that sends only a failure count has the count carried until the next upload.
- A run that no report was uploaded to fails (`no_results`).
- Migration `ci_run_evidence_union` (runs created before it keep their old key).

### Security: a CI run is bound to the job that exchanged its token

- Each CI run records the provider's job id from the verified OIDC token (GitHub `check_run_id`, GitLab `job_id`) next to the pipeline run id, attempt and actor login (migration `001137`, one column with a constant default).
- A run token is renewed only for that job and attempt: another job of the same pipeline, or a re-run, can no longer take over a running run's token; the attempt is refused and audited (`run_mismatch`).
- Every results upload is audited (`ci_run.results_uploaded`: finding count, tool label, job id; no finding content). Exchange audits carry the attempt, the job id and whether it was a renewal.
- The run view (`GET /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}`) returns `external_job_id`.

### Security: a CI run's reports are checked against the stored run, not the request's snapshot

- An upload now reserves one of the run's report slots in a single
  statement, only while the run is still running. Before, the status and
  the report count came from the snapshot taken when the run token was
  checked, so concurrent uploads (or the files of one ZIP) could pass the
  200-report cap, and a report could be recorded after the verdict.
- A verdict is stored only if no report was recorded while it was being
  computed; otherwise the run is judged again with that report (up to three
  times, then `409`).
- A report or a VEX document that arrives after the verdict is refused with
  `409` instead of being recorded without the verdict seeing it.

### Security: administrators are told about every CI break-glass and about bursts of refused CI tokens

- Creating a CI break-glass, and each run it lets pass, now notifies every active owner and administrator in-app and sends the new `ci.break_glass` notification event (on by default).
- The CI alert job raises `ci.token_refusals` (on by default, once while it lasts) when a tenant has at least 20 refused CI token exchanges in 30 minutes; it now also walks tenants that have a trust configuration but no pipeline yet.
- Migration `001111`: two event-type catalog rows and the `token_refusals` alert-state kind.

### Security: every CI trust audience names the organization

- GitHub and GitLab trust configurations now require an audience that contains the organization id, as Bitbucket, CircleCI and Jenkins already did. The default is `openctem:tenant:<id>`. A token minted for one organization is then useless to any other.
- Behaviour change: existing GitHub and GitLab configurations with another audience are moved to the default by migration `ci_tenant_bound_audience`.
- For 90 days, a pipeline that existed before the migration may still request the old audience, until it requests the new one once. A new pipeline must use the new audience.
- Otherwise the exchange is refused with `legacy_audience`. The trust card shows the old audience and its end date. Update pipelines to the current snippet.

### Security: a CI job's OIDC token re-exchanged gets the same run only, and refusals say why

- The same OIDC token presented again while valid (same bytes, same
  organization) gets a new upload token for the run it already opened or
  joined, and nothing wider: at most five exchanges per token, each audited
  with its count. Before, the second exchange was refused, so a job that lost
  the first answer, or ran `openctem-ci` more than once, could not report.
  Any other token under a used token id, or one presented to another
  organization, is still refused and audited at high severity (migration
  `002137`).
- A plain run's id is chosen at the first exchange: a re-exchange after a
  failed creation makes that run, never a second one.
- Refusals after the organization's trust configuration admitted the token
  now tell the pipeline the reason (`CI_TOKEN_REPLAY_LIMIT` with the first
  exchange time and run, `CI_TOKEN_REPLAY_RUN_CLOSED`, `CI_TOKEN_PIPELINE_RATE`
  and others). Refusals before admission stay one generic
  `CI_TOKEN_NOT_TRUSTED` that lists what to check, so a token from a stranger
  on a shared issuer learns nothing about the configuration.

### Security: changing CI trust needs a recent sign-in

- Creating or changing a CI trust configuration (`POST /api/v1/ci/trust-configs`, `PUT /api/v1/ci/trust-configs/{id}`) and changing the CI settings (`PUT /api/v1/ci/settings`) now need step-up, like a break-glass. A trust configuration decides which pipelines may send results that the gate judges, and the settings can let CI sensor keys back in. Without step-up, a stolen session could add the attacker's own CI organization.
- The console asks for the second factor and retries the request. Deleting a configuration only withdraws trust and is unchanged.

### Security: a CI trust can admit only the organization's central workflow

- **New trust rule `workflow_refs`** (GitHub and GitLab): a CI trust
  configuration can list the pipeline definitions it admits, as
  `<path>@<ref>` with a pattern in the ref. GitHub matches the token's
  `job_workflow_ref` (`acme/security/.github/workflows/scan.yml@refs/heads/main`),
  so only jobs that call the central reusable workflow report and get a
  verdict; a pull request that edits or adds a workflow file is refused with
  `workflow_not_allowed`. GitLab matches `ci_config_ref_uri`.
- A token without the claim is refused when the rule is set; the rule is
  refused on save for Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket, CircleCI and Jenkins, whose
  tokens do not name the definition. At most 20 entries; the path is exact.
- The trust preview shows the token's pipeline definition, and the CI/CD
  trust form and pipeline snippet show the rule.

### Security: a CI job can no longer choose the branch its findings are compared with

- A pull or merge request run took its baseline from the `base_ref` the job reported at the exchange (every
  GitLab merge request, every push run, CircleCI, Bitbucket, Jenkins), and any branch named `release/*` or
  `main` qualified. A developer could push `release/x` with a vulnerability and name it as the base of a merge
  request: the finding counted as pre-existing and the new-findings-only gate passed. The reported `base_ref`
  is now ignored. The baseline is GitHub's signed `base_ref`, or a GitLab merge request's target branch read
  from GitLab through the organization's GitLab connection, and only when that branch is the default branch or
  protected; otherwise the default branch.
- **Behaviour change:** a branch typed `main` or `release` from its name no longer counts as exposure for
  baselines or for promoting branch-only findings to organization findings; only the default branch and
  protected branches (from repository import or set by an administrator) do. Findings already promoted stay
  promoted. Migration `002147_exposure_default_or_protected_only` replaces `branch_counts_as_exposure`.
- **Upgrade note:** to compare merge requests into a release line with that line, mark the branch protected
  (repository import reads protection from the code host) and, for GitLab, connect the group.

### Security: probing jobs queued before scope records existed are re-checked at claim too

- Validate, retest and `connector_scan` jobs queued before the dispatch-gate record existed are re-checked at claim with their type's strict defaults (the full gate at t1, no act scope; no zone routing for a connector scan) instead of being handed out unchecked.
- One whose targets cannot be read from its payload is refused with the new failure code `GATE_RECORD_MISSING` (class `scope`, not retried); its validation run, retest or step is settled, and its owner creates it again.

### Security: validate, retest and connector scan jobs are re-checked against the current scope at claim

- The claim-time scope re-check now covers validate commands (finding re-checks, proof-of-fix, attack-simulation safe-checks), tool retests and `connector_scan` jobs (scan runs and coverage batches), not only scans. Each records the gate it passed at dispatch (`commands.dispatch_gate`, no new migration) and is re-checked with it when a sensor claims it.
- A job whose target is now refused fails with `SCOPE_CHANGED`, and what waits on it is settled as on a sensor failure: its validation run finishes as failed, its retest is settled, its scan step fails.
- Jobs of these types queued before the upgrade have no record: they are re-checked with their type's strict defaults (the full gate at t1, no act scope, no zone routing for a connector scan). One whose targets cannot be read is refused with `GATE_RECORD_MISSING` (its validation run, retest or step is settled) and has to be created again. Nothing queued before the upgrade goes out unchecked.

### Security: a scan job's targets are re-checked against the current scope when a sensor claims it

- A scan job can wait in the queue while its scope changes (an exclusion added, a scope entry removed or its tier lowered, an asset's ownership rejected, a scan zone deleted or shrunk, the actor's act scope revoked). The dispatch gate now runs again on every hand-out path (protocol v2 listing poll, claim-N and claim by id; protocol v3 `ClaimCommands` and claim), with the inputs the dispatch recorded (new column `commands.dispatch_gate`, migration 001352, platform-written only).
- Targets refused since dispatch are taken out of the job, in what the sensor gets and in the stored payload. A job left with no target is not handed out: it fails with `SCOPE_CHANGED` (also on its step, failure class `scope`, not retried), recorded once; a claim by id answers `command-claimed`.
- If the check cannot run, the job is withheld and stays pending (fail closed); the command expiry ends a job that can never be checked.
- **Upgrade note:** scan jobs queued before the upgrade have no record and are re-checked with the baseline rules (exclusions, rejected names, private-address and zone rules).

### Security: Sanitize request-derived log values and bound result-slice allocations
- Request-derived values and error text are passed through the log sanitizers before they are logged, so a crafted name or id cannot forge log lines.
- Result slices sized from a page size are now bounded by a constant capacity hint.

### Security: SAML login redirect validated, excelize bumped

- The SAML login redirect now refuses an IdP SSO URL that is not an absolute http(s) URL with a host and no credentials.
- Bumped excelize to a build that fixes the open CVEs in formula evaluation and the production web image upgrades zlib.

### Security: complete reports from a trusted collector may refresh its own assets

- A collector report names no command, so it could create assets but never change one, and a re-collected inventory refreshed nothing. Now a report with `coverage_type: full` from a collector of the organization at trust level `trusted` (push ingest in effect) may change the existing assets its own collector source (sensor, tool and `metadata.source_ref`) created, and when the report is committed the assets that source created and no longer lists are marked not seen (status `stale`, a `disappeared` history row). Nothing is ever deleted (RFC-040 §12).
- Never changed or marked: an asset another source or a person created, an asset with a person's manual attribute lock or manual status override, anything of another organization. A partial or incremental report never marks anything; an empty report, a report that lost assets on the way, or one that would drop more than half (and more than 100) of the source's assets marks nothing; an older report sent again cannot overwrite newer values or mark assets a newer report listed. A finding a person resolved stays resolved.
- Migration 002081 adds `collector_assets` (tenant-scoped, composite foreign keys to the asset and the sensor). Assets collectors created before it are not owned by any collector until the collector creates them again.

### Security: a scan command created through POST /commands is refused above its scope tier

- `POST /api/v1/commands` with type `scan` now applies the tier ceiling of a scan trigger: a target whose scope entries allow less than the named scanner probes at (its tier; T1 for an unknown scanner) refuses the command (`TARGET_OUT_OF_SCOPE`, 400, with `tier_exceeds` and the `raise_tier` fix), and a failed tier lookup refuses it.
- The command records that tier, so the claim-time scope re-check also catches a tier lowered while the command waits in the queue (`SCOPE_CHANGED`).

### Security: private package names no longer become shared catalog rows

- Software components move into the software catalog (RFC-070, migrations
  `components_on_software_catalog` and `drop_components_delete_permission`).
  The old global `components` table held one row per package URL and version
  for every tenant: a private package one organization reported
  (`pkg:npm/@acme/internal-auth`) became a shared row, and its description
  and homepage came from whichever organization reported it first. Every
  package an organization reports is now private to it; a shared package row
  exists only when the vulnerability feed names the package.
- A finding, a package link and a dependency edge can only reference the
  organization's own package versions or shared ones (database triggers).

### Security: least privilege for every Compose service

- Redis ran as root (a `sh -c` command skips the image's drop to the `redis`
  user); it now starts through the image's entrypoint and runs as uid 999.
  Existing `redis-data` volumes are re-owned on the first start.
- Postgres, Redis and the one-shot jobs (`datastore-tls`, `db-roles`,
  `migrate`) drop every capability and add back only what their entrypoints
  need; the gateway, `migrate`, `db-roles` and `datastore-tls` run with a
  read-only root filesystem; `datastore-tls` has no network. The Redis
  healthcheck reads the password from `REDISCLI_AUTH` instead of argv.

### Security: the console's CSRF token is bound to its session

- The platform console's CSRF token is now HMAC-SHA256 of the console session under a server key derived from `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` (shared by the replicas), and the API verifies that binding on every console write instead of comparing the header with the `admin_csrf` cookie. A cookie planted by a script on another site of the same host (cookies ignore ports) can no longer satisfy the check.
- Every `/api/v1/admin` response, the sign-in and validate responses included, is `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- **Upgrade note:** a console tab open when this ships gets 401 on its next change; reloading the page (which fetches the bound token from validate) or signing in again fixes it.

### Security: in production the console needs a CSRF secret shared by every replica

- The console's CSRF tokens are signed with a key derived from the session
  secret (`AUTH_JWT_SECRET`, or `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` when it is derived). In
  production the API now refuses to start without one, instead of drawing a
  per-process random key that breaks the token on the next replica. With
  `AUTH_PROVIDER=oidc` set `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` explicitly.

### Security: a second super admin approves the console's most dangerous actions

- Making or removing a super admin, turning off the security-key requirement, removing or relaxing the administrators' identity provider, opening sign-up and re-signing an organization's audit chain now need another super admin's approval when one exists. The protected route answers `428 SECOND_APPROVAL_REQUIRED`; the console asks for the approval (reason, step-up), another super admin approves under Security > Approvals (fresh step-up), and the requester repeats the action within 24 hours. An approval is bound to its requester, action and exact target, works once and expires; nobody approves their own request (also a table constraint); break-glass accounts never approve and do not count as a second super admin. Every step is audited critical and e-mailed to the administrators.
- With one named super admin the actions run on that admin's step-up alone, audited critical (`approval.single_admin`) and announced; the Approvals page explains how to add a second super admin.
- Migration `002914_admin_approvals` adds the `admin_approvals` table (new, empty; safe on a populated database).
- **Upgrade note:** installations that run the console with its own database role (`DB_ADMIN_USER`) re-run the role script (`deploy/postgres/least-privilege-roles.sql` with `admin_user`, or `db-grants`) so the console role gets `admin_approvals` and the app role loses it. Installations with two or more named super admins should expect the approval step on these actions from this release.

### Security: platform console hardening (sessions, write-ahead audit, administrator accounts off the main site)

- An administrator may hold at most three verified console sessions; opening another ends the oldest (`console.session_evicted` in the administrators' audit log).
- A super administrator's write is recorded (`admin.write_started`, with the redacted request body) before it runs. If the audit log cannot be written the request is refused with 503 `AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE` and nothing changes.
- The audit redaction of request bodies also covers keys ending in `secret`, `password`, `_key` or `_token` (any case) and the keys `code`, `totp`, `recovery_code`, `recovery_codes`, including inside lists.
- The account of a platform administrator can no longer sign in on the tenant site (password, second factor, token exchange, social and SSO sign-in). The answer is the same as for a wrong password, with no session; the console's own sign-in is unchanged. The sign-in page tells administrators to use the admin console.
- The console's sign-in steps use their own page cookie `console_csrf` instead of the tenant site's `csrf_token`, so the two sites no longer overwrite each other's token on one host.
- The gateway's console site sends `Strict-Transport-Security` on proxied responses.
- Upgrade note: with `MANAGED_SERVICE=true` and `APP_ENV=production` the API now refuses to start unless `ADMIN_AUDIT_SINK` is set (an https, syslog+tls or file destination). Set it before upgrading a managed deployment; self-managed installations are unaffected.

### Security: the platform console's identity tables can get their own database role

- New optional `DB_ADMIN_USER` / `DB_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. With it, the
  least-privilege bootstrap (`-v admin_user=...`) creates a console role that
  alone writes `admin_users`, `admin_credentials`, `admin_sessions`,
  `platform_identity_provider` and `admin_idp_login_states`; the API's
  `DB_USER` keeps only `SELECT` on `admin_users`. The API opens a second small
  pool with it for the console's repositories, so a SQL injection in the tenant
  plane cannot add an administrator or read a console session.
- Compose: `db-roles` passes `admin_user` when `DB_ADMIN_USER` is set, and a new
  `db-grants` job reruns the script after `migrate`, before the API, so a table
  a migration just created gets its grants on the same `up`.
  `deploy/.env.example` and `setup.sh` set the role up for new installations;
  existing ones are unchanged until they add the two variables.
- The console role holds only what the console's repositories touch: full DML
  on its identity tables, insert and read on `admin_audit_logs`, read on the
  audit chain anchors and `tenant_members`, read and update on `users`. It
  cannot read or write tenant data.
- `bootstrap-admin` and `rekey` connect as the schema owner (`DB_MIGRATE_USER`)
  when it is set.
- The API logs an error at start-up when `DB_ADMIN_USER` is set but the app
  role can still write `admin_users`.

### Security: console sessions end after 15 minutes without use

- A verified platform console session now ends after 15 minutes without use (was 30); the absolute lifetime stays 8 hours. Fifteen minutes is the inactivity bound for the highest authenticator assurance level, and the console is the instance's most powerful surface (RFC-022 revision 21).

### Security: the platform console is its own service, at the root of its own site

- The console is now its own web app and image, `ghcr.io/openctemio/openctem-console` (web/console in the repository), served by the gateway's console site at its root: `https://<host>:8443/` (port mode, the default) or `https://<OPENCTEM_ADMIN_HOST>/` (host mode, recommended for production). The tenant web app (`openctem-web`) contains no console page, route or API proxy, refuses to proxy `/api/v1/admin` however it is spelled, and the console contains no tenant page. There is no `/admin` path any more, and no redirect from it.
- The console sends strict headers on every response: a nonce Content-Security-Policy with `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`, `form-action 'self'` and no third-party script (only the sign-in CAPTCHA frame), `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`, `Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- The Compose stack runs it as the `console` service (`CONSOLE_IMAGE`, `CONSOLE_VERSION`, `CONSOLE_MEMORY_LIMIT`); the gateway reaches it at `OPENCTEM_CONSOLE_UPSTREAM` (default `console:3000`). `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_PLANE` and the `X-OpenCTEM-Plane` header are removed, and the web service no longer takes `ADMIN_API_URL`.
- A platform administrator who signs in on the tenant sign-in page is told to use the console instead of being sent to `/admin`.
- **Upgrade note:** open the console at the root of its site (bookmarks to `/admin/...` drop the `/admin` prefix). A platform identity provider's redirect URI becomes `<console origin>/login/callback`. Deployments other than this Compose file add the console service (the Helm chart and the Ansible kit do in their own releases).

### Security: platform console security keys and passkeys

- Platform administrators can register security keys and passkeys (WebAuthn, user verification required) and use them to sign in to the console and to confirm protected actions; the console offers them before the authenticator-app code. The relying party is the console's own origin (`ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL`, default the origin of `APP_URL`), so an assertion from the tenant site or a look-alike domain is refused.
- Ten one-time recovery codes per administrator, shown once and regenerated with a step-up.
- New console policy "require security keys" (System > Admin sign-in, super admin with step-up). It turns on only when the administrator turning it on has at least two keys and recovery codes; other administrators keep signing in but reach only the enrollment page until they comply, the last two keys cannot be removed, and the authenticator-app code is refused for an administrator who holds a key (break-glass administrators keep it). Reset credentials also removes keys and recovery codes.
- Upgrade note: additive migration (`admin_webauthn_credentials`, `admin_recovery_codes`, `admin_webauthn_ceremonies`). Set `ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL` to the console site (`https://<OPENCTEM_ADMIN_HOST>` or `https://<host>:8444`) when the console has its own site; changing it later makes registered keys unusable.
- Adding a key, regenerating recovery codes, changing the require-keys policy and owner create or recovery each demand a fresh code or a just-given, single-use security-key confirmation, never the five-minute step-up window. Every key added and every recovery-code regeneration emails the administrator. When the policy is switched on, administrators without a key keep the authenticator-app code for 7 days (the deadline is shown in the console), then are refused.

### Security: platform console sessions idle out and roster changes are announced

- An open console tab no longer stays signed in for the full 8 hours: the
  console's own periodic refreshes carry `X-Admin-Background: 1` and do not
  count as activity, so a tab nobody uses signs out after 15 minutes.
- A password reset or change, or a two-step reset, of a platform
  administrator's account now also ends that administrator's console
  sessions (audited as `console.sessions_ended_by_account`).
- Adding, changing or removing an administrator, resetting one's console
  sign-in, changing the administrators' identity provider or the
  security-key policy is emailed to every other active administrator and
  logged with `alert=admin_roster_change`.
- Publishing or ending an announcement, changing an organization's limits or
  idle policy, turning a threat-intelligence feed on or off, and blocking or
  unblocking an AI application now ask for a step-up.
- The console sends `Strict-Transport-Security`, and its API proxy no longer
  shows network error details when the API cannot be reached.

### Security: content package signatures, signed index and revocation list

- `pkg/contentpkg` verifies offline bundles of content packages (RFC-099): a catalog key set signed by an offline
  root pinned in the release, a catalog countersignature per package version, the publisher's keyless Sigstore
  signature over the artifact (checked offline against the bundled Sigstore trusted root, with the build identity
  and issuer matched exactly), a signed index with a sequence (no rollback) and an expiry (no freeze), and a
  signed revocation list (by package, version or digest) that works without network access.
- Unsigned, tampered, expired, rolled-back and revoked content is refused; there is no switch to accept it.
- Adds the `github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go` dependency. No behaviour change yet: the catalog that uses it follows.

### Security: scan coverage closes findings only on the assets its command covers

- A scan run that reports full coverage (`INGEST_COVERAGE_AUTO_RESOLVE=enforce`) closed the open findings of its tool on every existing asset its report named, including assets the command was never sent to scan. A compromised sensor could close real findings anywhere in its organization by naming their assets in a report. Coverage is now limited to the assets the command targets cover, as repository runs already were. In the default `dry_run` mode the would-be closures shrink the same way.

### Security: an undecryptable stored credential is never used as is

- Integration credentials (SCM, notification webhooks, Telegram, SMTP,
  Splunk), Jira and GitHub ticketing credentials and the Jira/GitHub inbound
  webhook secret fell back to the stored value when it did not decrypt under
  `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. After a key mismatch that sent ciphertext upstream, and
  a legacy plaintext row was used unencrypted (RFC-049 F-8). They now fail
  closed: the integration reports "stored credentials cannot be decrypted with
  the configured key" (HTTP 424 on the integration endpoints), ticketing skips
  the integration, and an undecryptable webhook secret verifies nothing.
- `APP_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_CREDENTIALS` (development without a key) is unchanged.
- **Upgrade note:** run `cmd/encrypt-credentials` before upgrading if any
  integration still holds a plaintext credential (it lists them with
  `-dry-run`); re-enter or re-key any credential the current key does not open.

### Security: custom template trust (RFC-038 §6.12)

- **Custom templates reach sensors only in a signed manifest.** Every
  command poll signs one DSSE envelope per command (Ed25519 over the exact
  bytes) listing the tenant, the polling sensor, the command, a 1-hour
  expiry and the SHA-256 of every template; templates are validated again
  first, and a set that fails is sent unsigned so the sensor refuses it.
  Keys are per tenant, derived from `APP_TEMPLATE_SIGNING_KEY` (new;
  unset: derived from `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`). New
  `GET /api/v1/scanner-templates/signing-key` returns the tenant's public
  key to pin on its sensors (`SENSOR_TEMPLATE_SIGNING_KEYS`). **Upgrade
  note:** sensors on the matching sdk-go refuse custom templates until the
  key is pinned; scans without custom templates are unaffected.
- **More nuclei protocols refused at upload.** The `file` protocol (reads
  the sensor's disk) and self-contained templates are refused like `code`,
  `javascript` and `headless` already were, with an error naming the
  protocol.

### Security: dashboards no longer show pentest findings to non-members, and executive top risks follow the viewer's own scope

- **Pentest visibility on every dashboard query.** Recent activity (finding
  titles and messages), the executive top risks, the finding counts, the
  monthly trend, the velocity and the executive totals now apply the same
  pentest member-visibility rule as the findings list for everyone who is not
  an organization administrator: a pentest finding is counted or shown only to
  a member of its campaign, and never as a draft or in-review finding to the
  campaign's client role. Before, a member whose scope covered the tested
  asset, or a full-data role, could read pentest finding titles, including
  unpublished drafts, on the dashboard. The rule is one shared helper
  (`vulnerability.FindingMemberVisibilitySQL`) used by the findings list and
  the dashboards.
- Recent activity, the monthly trend, velocity and the executive
  new-finding count leave out unpublished pentest findings (draft, in review)
  for all callers.
- **Top risks for an aggregate viewer.** A restricted viewer holding
  `dashboard:aggregate` now gets their own top five open findings (computed
  with their row scope) instead of the organization's top five filtered down,
  which usually left the list empty. Their totals stay organization-wide with
  the existing k-floor.

### Security: threat-intel, validation, program-metrics and cycle figures follow the viewer; dashboards fail closed

- The tenant EPSS and KEV exposure counts, the validation coverage and
  downgrade figures and the program metrics now apply the pentest
  member-visibility rule of the findings list: a pentest finding counts only
  for a member of its campaign, and a draft or in-review one counts for nobody.
  Before, a viewer whose scope covered the tested asset could count (and, by
  differencing, infer) pentest findings of campaigns they were not on.
- `GET /ctem-cycles` and `GET /ctem-cycles/{id}` (and the close and
  scope-refinement responses) omit `charter_evaluation`, which is computed from
  organization-wide metrics, for a restricted viewer without
  `dashboard:aggregate`; the rest of the cycle stays readable.
- The dashboard counts take the `dashboard:aggregate` decision from the
  data-scope enforcer only (one wiring instead of two), and the dashboard,
  attack-path and exposure-chain reads for a caller refuse when the enforcer is
  not wired instead of returning organization-wide data.

### Security: threat intel, validation, scan coverage, CTEM cycle and attack-path summaries respect the viewer's data scope

- `GET /threat-intel/stats` (EPSS and KEV past-due counts), `GET /validation/coverage`,
  `GET /scans/coverage` and the `summary` of `GET /attack-surface/attack-paths`
  counted the whole organization for a restricted member, so a member with
  no assets in scope still saw the organization's exposure numbers. They now
  count the findings and assets the caller may see; a viewer with
  `dashboard:aggregate` or full data access gets the organization totals, as on
  `/dashboard/stats`. The attack-path rows stay limited to the caller's scope
  for everyone.
- `GET /ctem-cycles/metrics/trend` is computed per organization and cannot be
  narrowed: a restricted member without `dashboard:aggregate` or full data
  access now gets 403.

### Security: dashboards, MCP and suppression rules follow the caller's data scope

- **Dashboards.** The weekly velocity, the executive summary totals, the data
  quality scorecard and the process metrics count the viewer's own scope, like
  `/dashboard/stats` (a restricted member without `dashboard:aggregate` saw
  organization totals). A viewer with `dashboard:aggregate` or full data access
  still sees the organization. The risk-trend history and the program metrics
  are kept for the whole organization: a restricted viewer without
  `dashboard:aggregate` gets an empty trend and a 403 on the program metrics.
- **MCP finding tools.** The by-id read behind `get_finding`,
  `explain_priority`, `list_finding_transitions` and `add_finding_comment` makes
  the same decision as the REST route guard. A full-data role no longer reads
  the findings of a private bug-bounty program it is not a member of.
- **Suppression rules.** A rule bound to an asset is read, edited, approved and
  deleted only by a caller whose scope holds the asset, and the list leaves out
  the others. An organization-wide rule needs full data access to create, edit,
  approve, delete or mark reviewed (a restricted member with
  `findings:suppressions:approve` could approve a rule that closes findings on
  every asset). The active-rules list of the user route (`/suppressions/active`)
  leaves out rules bound to assets outside the caller's scope; the sensor route
  is unchanged.

### Security: data scope follows group and rule changes in the same transaction

- `user_accessible_assets` is now kept in step with its sources by database
  triggers, in the writing transaction (migration **001051**, RFC-050 W6):
  group asset assign/unassign, a member leaving a group, a group deactivated,
  re-activated or deleted, a scope rule deactivated or deleted. Before, a
  deactivated or deleted access group kept granting its assets indefinitely,
  a deactivated or narrowed scope rule kept what it had granted, and a deleted rule's rows were orphaned.
- Narrowing or deactivating a scope rule reconciles the whole group (stale
  auto-assignments removed); an asset-group membership change reconciles the
  rules of its tenant (the lookup used a zero tenant id and never matched, M-3).
- The migration removes the rows of rules that are already deactivated and
  runs one full refresh to repair scope rows left by the old behaviour.

### Security: outbound requests refuse IPv6 site-local addresses; one internal-address list checked everywhere

- `pkg/httpsec` now always blocks `fec0::/10` (deprecated IPv6 site-local), which ctis addrscope, the deny list the sensors use, already treats as internal.
- Security lint rule 6 checks the API's blocked ranges against ctis addrscope itself now that sdk-go takes its deny list from it: every addrscope range must be blocked by the API, and the API may block nothing addrscope does not name. A missing ctis module fails the rule.
