- CI jobs on Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines, CircleCI and Jenkins (OpenID Connect provider plugin) exchange their OIDC token for a run token, like GitHub Actions and GitLab CI. Each trust names one CI organization, workspace or controller; there is no wildcard issuer.
- Per provider: Azure tokens must carry the issuer's `org_id`; Bitbucket trust pins the workspace UUID and lists repositories by UUID, and a reported repository name stays bound to the first repository UUID that used it; CircleCI SSH re-runs are refused; pull request builds on Azure, CircleCI and Jenkins are refused unless fork pull requests are admitted (their tokens cannot tell a fork's). Bitbucket, CircleCI and Jenkins audiences must contain the organization id.
- Tokens without a `jti` (Bitbucket, CircleCI, Jenkins) are accepted once by the token's hash.
- A commit the token does not sign (CircleCI, Jenkins without a `sha` claim) is the job's report: the run marks it unverified (`ci_runs.commit_verified`, migration `001261`) and a break-glass never applies to it.
- `POST /api/v1/ci/trust-configs/preview` (`scans:ci:write`, rate limited): verifies a sample token against a draft trust and shows its claims and whether the rules admit it; nothing is stored.

### Added: CI pipelines in the fleet

- Each workflow file of each repository that runs with CI OIDC is now a CI pipeline (migration `001084`), keyed by the provider's immutable repository id and the workflow path from the verified token, so renames and branches never add rows. Pipelines are created only at an admitted exchange, capped per organization (2,000) and per trust configuration (1,000), and audited (`ci_pipeline.created`).
- A pipeline's status is fresh, stale (two missed scheduled cycles, or three times its usual interval, 7 to 30 days), archived (90 days idle), failing (last default-branch verdict), degraded (scanner errors, runner below `SENSOR_MIN_VERSION`) or revoked; never offline. Fork runs attach to the upstream pipeline and never change its status.
- New read endpoints: `GET /api/v1/fleet?mode=all|daemon|runner` (sensors and CI pipelines in one list, each mode under its own permission), `GET /api/v1/ci/pipelines`, `GET /api/v1/ci/pipelines/{id}`, and `pipeline_id` on `GET /api/v1/ci/runs`.
- Existing runs are backfilled into pipelines; the first verified run of each adopts it.

### Added: an AppSec custom role can run the CI gate

- New permission `scans:ci:policy`: create, change and delete CI gate policies and coverage expectations. The routes that need it are `POST`/`PATCH`/`DELETE /api/v1/ci/gate-policies` and `PUT`/`DELETE /api/v1/ci/coverage/expectations/{id}`; they needed `scans:ci:write` before. The owner and admin roles get it, so nothing changes for them.
- `scans:ci:override` (break-glass) can now be put on a custom role. It still needs step-up, and every administrator is alerted when it is used.
- `scans:ci:write` (trust configurations, CI settings, code host connections) stays admin-only: these issue or admit upload credentials.
- The AppSec engineer role template carries `scans:ci:read`, `scans:ci:policy` and `scans:ci:override`.

### Added: a repository's .openctem.yml can tighten the CI gate and request exceptions

- `POST /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}/evaluate` takes `repo_policy` (the gate part of
  the repository's `.openctem.yml`, sent by the runner). Its values apply only
  when stricter than the organization's policy (`fail_on_severity`,
  `new_findings_only: false`, `fail_on_kev: true`, `epss_threshold`,
  `block_rules`); an invalid file is refused. The verdict says
  `repo_file: applied` or `ignored`.
- `exceptions` (rule, optional path, reason, expiry within 90 days) become
  pending suppression requests on the repository, from default-branch runs
  only and once each (audited `ci_run.exceptions_requested`); they apply only
  after an administrator approves them.
- A gate policy with `allow_repo_policy: false` makes the platform ignore
  repository files (any applicable policy saying no wins). Migration
  `ci_gate_policy_allow_repo_policy`.

### Added: CI gate settings and baseline in the console, per repository

- A CI pipeline's drawer has a Settings tab: every gate field of its repository with the effective value,
  where it comes from (default, organization, business unit or this repository), the inherited value of an
  override, and the locks set above. Users with the CI gate policy permission override a field or reset it to
  the inherited value; a locked field offers only stricter values, and a change that loosens the gate asks
  for a reason (10 to 500 characters) and an optional end date (within 365 days). Readers see it read only.
- The same tab shows the gate baseline (when, how, by whom, branch, findings, when it blocks again) with
  "Record baseline now" and "Remove baseline", and links to the audit log for the repository's history.
- The pipelines list has a "Has overrides" filter (`?overrides=1`).
- The organization and business unit gate policy dialog locks fields, edits the baseline settings and shows
  how many repositories override each field, with a link to them. Saving keeps the baseline grace days,
  reason and end date, which every write replaces.
- A CI run's drawer splits findings into baseline (not blocking) and new, announces a baseline recorded on the
  first run with its due date, offers "Connect GitLab" (or "Install the GitHub App") when the check could not
  be posted for lack of a connection, and runs of the same commit are labelled "Attempt N of M".
- Deleting a business unit or repository gate policy asks for a reason, which the API requires when the deletion loosens the gate; resetting a repository's last override does too.

### Added: a CI run can upload a tool's output file

- `POST /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}/results` also takes a file a tool wrote in any format the importers read (an SBOM, OSV scanner results, a DefectDojo export, a VEX document, ...) or a ZIP of them, detected from the content; CTIS stays the default. It goes through the same conversion and limits as the finding import.
- Everything is filed on the run's repository with the branch, commit and pull request of the verified token; findings the file puts on another asset are dropped and counted (`findings_dropped_out_of_scope`); VEX statements are stored on the repository's findings only and never close one.
- SARIF 2.1.0 (also marked by `Content-Type: application/sarif+json`), semgrep, trivy, grype, gitleaks, nuclei and ZAP files are converted on the run's repository: the importer files code reports on the run's repository and branch whatever the file names (SARIF `versionControlProvenance` included), and a record that names no asset goes there too. A report is taken for CTIS only when it has a `metadata` object (or comes as `{"report": ...}`), so a SARIF or semgrep file with a `version` member no longer falls to the CTIS decoder.

### Added: the CI run detail shows how the verdict came about and whether it reached the code host

- `GET /api/v1/ci/runs` and `GET /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}` now return:
  - `would_fail`: the pass came only from a warn policy or a break-glass;
  - `override`: the break-glass override that let the commit pass;
  - `decoration_state` and `decoration_detail`: whether the gate check and pull request comment were posted, are waiting, or failed, with a short reason.
- Console, CI/CD → Runs:
  - running runs and passes that would have failed are marked in the list;
  - the open run is kept in the URL (`?run=`);
  - the run detail separates blocking reasons from comment-only ones and counts monitored findings;
  - it says when a break-glass let the commit pass (who, why, until when);
  - it shows the check and comment status, the tools, scan failures, the `.openctem.yml` outcome, whether the commit was signed by the CI provider, when the run was judged, and a link to the run's findings;
  - administrators can open a prefilled break-glass for a failed run's commit.

### Added: CI pipelines authenticate with their OIDC token and ask a central gate (RFC-051)

- `POST /api/v1/ci/oidc/exchange`: a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job exchanges its OIDC token, checked against the organization's CI trust configurations, for a run upload token that expires within 15 minutes and is bound to one run on one repository asset. Fork pull requests get none by default; each OIDC token is exchanged once; every exchange is audited.
- `POST /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}/results` and `/evaluate`: upload results for the run's repository only, then get pass or fail with reasons and links from the gate policy (repository, business unit, organization, default): new findings only against the default branch, accepted risk honored, committed secrets always fail. Audited break-glass per commit.
- CI runs are not sensors: the console lists them under CI runners; trust, gate policy and break-glass are under Settings > Scanning > CI pipelines.
- Permissions `scans:ci:read` (all system roles), `scans:ci:write` and `scans:ci:override` (owner and admin only; refused on custom roles). Migration `001077`.

### Added: A CI trust adds the repositories it trusts to scope

- With "Trust and add to scope" (`manage_scope`), a GitHub (github.com, GitHub Enterprise Server) or GitLab (gitlab.com, self-managed) trust adds a linked repository scope entry for each owner (`<host>/<owner>/*`) or repository it trusts. Other providers name their code host per run and do not.
- The entries are created as the person who saves the trust, through the same scope decision as adding them by hand. With scan approval off they are in effect at once; under Strict, an approver's entries wait for their approvals and anyone else's are not added. Administrators are told, as for any widening.
- An equal entry that already exists is linked, never duplicated, and stays the person's. Entries the trust created (origin `ci_trust`) follow the trust: an edit moves them, disabling or deleting the trust retires them, and two trusts on one namespace share one entry until the last goes.
- The first verified pipeline run under a pattern is recorded as evidence (`scope_entries[].seen_*` on the trust, `managed_by[]` on the scope entry). A legacy-audience run never counts. A run never creates an entry; it may only link an existing equal one.
- Opt-in governance: the scope setting `ci_scope_requires_proof` (default off) keeps a trust's new entries inactive until a verified run under them. That run puts an entry into effect only while the organization needs no approvals for it at that moment; if scan approval turned Strict in the meantime, the entry waits for its approvals and administrators are told.
- Security: `manage_scope` needs `attack_surface:scope:write` (403 `MANAGE_SCOPE_FORBIDDEN`). Without it the default is off, and such a caller may rename or narrow a trust, never widen its scope. An entry a trust manages answers 409 `CI_TRUST_MANAGED` to scope edits of its tier, expiry, reason or discovery, and to activate, deactivate and delete; change the trust or add an exclusion. An existing entry a person deletes is recorded on the link (`removed_at`) and is never created again by the trust. Links are tenant-scoped with composite foreign keys.
- Migration `002193_ci_trust_managed_scope` adds `ci_trust_configs.manage_scope` (existing trusts stay off; an administrator turns it on per trust), the origin `ci_trust` and the table `scope_target_ci_trusts`.

### Added: Dry run for adding existing CI trusts' repositories to scope

- CI trusts saved before "Trust and add to scope" existed keep it off. Nothing adds their repositories automatically: an administrator who may change scope turns it on per trust. That change is audited and the entries follow the organization's approval rules.
- New read-only command `ci-trust-scope-plan` in the API image, per tenant and in total:
  - what turning it on would do for those trusts (entries to create, or equal entries to link);
  - what the trusts that already manage scope would change (create, link, keep, retire, entries a person removed);
  - the patterns the platform would refuse.
- It runs on a read-only connection, so it is safe on a live database: `docker compose exec api /app/ci-trust-scope-plan` (`-tenant <id>`, `-json`).

### Added: CI trust and scope in the console

- The CI trust form has "Trust and add to scope". It is on by default for someone who may change scope, and off and explained for anyone else.
- Each trust card lists its repository scope entries. Each entry shows "Seen in a verified pipeline" (with the repository and time) or "No verified pipeline yet", and says when a person removed it or when it is waiting or could not be added.
- A trust saved before the option existed offers "Add these repositories to scope" to someone who may change scope.
- On Scoping, an entry a CI trust manages says "Managed by the CI trust …" with its evidence. Its only action is to open the trust. Every repository entry offers "Set up CI for these repositories".
- Scoping › Settings has the opt-in "Require proof for CI scopes".
- The trust list API returns every trust's `scope_entries` from one read. For a caller whose data scope does not reach the evidence's repository, its repository and run are left out (the time stays), on the list and the detail alike. The scope entry's `managed_by` no longer names the repository.

### Added: an alert when a pull request is merged without a passing CI gate

- When a default-branch run on GitHub comes from a merged pull request whose
  last OpenCTEM gate verdict was not a pass (or that was never judged), the
  notification event `ci.ungated_merge` is sent (high, once per run;
  migration `event_type_ci_ungated_merge`). It needs the GitHub App
  installation that posts the check; it tells you a merge did not wait for the
  gate, typically because the check is not required in branch protection.

### Added: `Idempotency-Key` on the CI upload endpoint

- `POST /api/v1/ci/runs/{id}/results` accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header. A retry of the same request (same key and body, same run) after a lost response gets the first answer back (`Idempotent-Replayed: true`) instead of ingesting the report again and counting another report. The key is scoped to the tenant and run, stored for one hour; the same key with another body is `422`, a key still in flight is `409` with `Retry-After`. Without Redis the header is ignored.

### Added: dispatch metrics: claim latency, queue depth by stage and wait reason, wait until claimed

- `command_claim_duration_seconds{mode}`, `command_claim_wait_seconds{class}` and `command_claim_skipped_total{reason}` (`local_policy`, `no_slot`, `scope_changed`, `window_hold`, `program_hold`, `taken`) show how long claims take, how long work waits for a sensor and why poll candidates were not handed out.
- `openctem_command_queue_depth{stage,tool,class,wait}` counts pending commands by stage, platform tool, priority and wait reason (`ready`, `host_busy`, `scheduled`); `openctem_command_queue_tenants` and `openctem_command_queue_top_tenant_pending` give the tenant dimension without tenant identity. A tenant's own tool is reported as `_custom`.
- The "OpenCTEM operations" Grafana dashboard has a new Dispatch row with these series.

### Added: `refingerprint -clear-legacy-secret-fingerprints`

- Secret findings created before the keyed fingerprint carry a value computed from the tenant id alone, which cannot be verified and is never rewritten. The new tool mode clears them in batches without long locks (dry run by default, `-apply` to commit, `-before` and `-tenant` to narrow it), so the next sighting writes the keyed value. A secret seen again may open one new finding next to the cleared one; see `docs/deployment/encryption-key-rotation.md`.

### Added: code scanning settings, protected branches and the baseline of each branch

- CI/CD gains code scanning of repositories (RFC-091), with an organization template that repositories inherit and per-repository overrides. The settings are:
  - protected branches: the default branch and `develop` by default, names or `release/*` patterns, at most 20;
  - capabilities: SAST, secrets, SCA, IaC;
  - the full rescan schedule (weekly by default);
  - routing;
  - on or off.
- Each branch records its baseline: none, queued, running, done (with the commit and date) or failed, and the trigger of its last full scan.
- `POST /api/v1/ci/code-scanning/repositories/{id}/baseline` sets a new baseline: it queues a full scan of a repository's protected branches. The scans themselves run on sensors in a later change.
- API: `GET/PUT /api/v1/ci/code-scanning/settings`, `GET /api/v1/ci/code-scanning/repositories[/{id}]`, `PUT/DELETE /api/v1/ci/code-scanning/repositories/{id}/settings`. Reading needs `scans:ci:read`; changes need `scans:ci:write` and are audited. Repositories outside the caller's data scope answer 404 and are not listed.
- Migration `code_scan_settings`: a new table, and new columns on `repository_branches` with constant defaults (no table rewrite).

### Added: the codeql tool row

- Migration 001169 adds the built-in `codeql` row to `tools`. The sensor ships codeql and the scan-stage catalog routes `sast.code` to it, but without a row tenants could neither enable it nor see whether their sensors have it (RFC-055, D9).
- An existing platform `codeql` row is left as it is. The down migration removes only the row this migration added.

### Added: an asset's last-seen time comes from the source's own last_seen

- A report asset's `last_seen` property (RFC 3339, `YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss` UTC, or Unix seconds) is the time the asset was last seen, when it is earlier than the report's time and not before 2000; otherwise the report's time is used. The stored last-seen time never moves backwards, and an observation older than it never reactivates a stale or inactive asset (`Asset.ObserveAt`).

### Added: collector placement is stored as asset relationships

- A report's typed `relationships` (CTIS) become asset relationships when the registry allows the pair: `hosted_by` is stored as `runs_on` (a virtual machine on its hypervisor host, a service on a host) or, for an address, as the host `contains` the address; `subdomain_of` is stored parent first as `contains`; `resolves_to`, `cname_of`, `exposes` and `serves_certificate` keep their type.
- A virtual machine whose report names its hypervisor host (`esxi_host`, sent by the vCenter collector) gets a `runs_on` edge to that host, and a reported host gets a `contains` edge to each existing address asset of its `ip_addresses` (at most 32; addresses are never created from a host's properties).
- Both ends are always assets of the reporting tenant, an edge is added only when the report may change its source asset (an unsolicited report adds none to an existing asset), and writing an edge again only refreshes when it was last seen.
- The relationship registry now allows `host runs_on host` and `host contains ip_address`.

### Added: any command's logs can be read

- `GET /api/v1/commands/{id}/logs` returns the log lines a sensor sent for any command (scan, retest, validate, connector, system), not only for the tasks of a scan run. It returns at most 5,000 lines, oldest first, kept 14 days.
- It is gated by `commands:read`, like the command itself.
- A command about a finding (a retest's commands, a validate job) also needs `findings:read` and the finding in the caller's data scope; otherwise it is not found.
- Another organization's command is not found.

### Added: task budgets, per-command progress and stall detection

- Every scan command carries a layered budget (`budget`: per-target, task and
  stall seconds) from per-tool defaults. A sensor on sdk-go with task budgets
  bounds each target with it and stops a task only at twice its budget.
- Sensors report each held command's finished targets on the heartbeat
  (feature `command_progress`). A running task that finishes no target for
  its stall window, or runs past twice its budget, is re-queued like a lost
  lease (`commands_stalled_total`); a slow but progressing task is left alone.
- The run's task list returns `progress` (`done`, `total`,
  `last_progress_at`), `budget_seconds` and `stall_seconds`.

### Added: software components API

- `GET /api/v1/components` lists packages (one row per package) with versions
  in use, assets, open findings by severity, KEV, fix availability, licenses
  and risk; server-side filters, sorting, pagination and facets.
- `GET /api/v1/components/summary`, `GET /api/v1/components/{id}`,
  `/{id}/versions` (with upgrade advice), `/{id}/assets` (where used),
  `/{id}/vulnerabilities`; `GET /api/v1/assets/{id}/dependency-paths` and
  `/dependency-graph` (bounded).
- `POST /api/v1/components/import?dry_run=true` previews an SBOM (counts,
  skipped entries with reasons, the difference with the current inventory)
  without writing; the import reads the CycloneDX dependency graph and SPDX
  relationships.

### Added: compose overlay for a bundled sensor enrolled as a shared sensor

- `api/deploy/docker-compose.sensor.yml` runs a sensor next to the stack that enrolls as a shared sensor of the instance. A one-shot `sensor-enrollment` service registers `SENSOR_INSTANCE_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN` (`bootstrap-admin sensor-token`, valid one hour, single use) after the migrations; the sensor enrolls with it on first start and keeps its identity in the `sensor-data` volume.
- The sensor runs in shared mode (`SENSOR_SHARED_MODE=1`, sandbox and network confinement required, the local policy `./sensor/sensor-policy.yaml` required), with no capability added (`cap_drop: ALL`, no-new-privileges, read-only root) and the sensor release's seccomp profile (`sensor/seccomp.json`: Docker's default plus clone/unshare with namespace flags, for its per-task user, network and mount namespaces). Shared jobs reach only a sensor that advertises `shared.isolation@1`; a sensor image without shared mode enrolls but receives none.
- `setup.sh` writes a generated `SENSOR_INSTANCE_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN` (`octe_` and 49 letters or digits) into a new `.env`, and copies `sensor/sensor-policy.example.yaml` (public targets only) to `sensor/sensor-policy.yaml`.
- **Upgrade note:** the overlay is opt-in. An existing install whose sensor was paired as an organization sensor keeps it; add `SENSOR_INSTANCE_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN` to `.env` (octe_ and 49 letters or digits) only to start the overlay.

### Added: the product brand is configuration

- `BRAND_NAME`, `BRAND_SHORT_NAME`, `BRAND_PRIMARY_COLOR`, the documentation,
  website, support, terms and privacy links, `BRAND_SUPPORT_EMAIL`,
  `BRAND_EMAIL_FOOTER`, `BRAND_POWERED_BY` and the logo and favicon files
  (`BRAND_LOGO_LIGHT_FILE`, `BRAND_LOGO_DARK_FILE`, `BRAND_FAVICON_FILE`), or
  one YAML `BRAND_FILE`, set the brand users see. Unset, everything stays
  OpenCTEM.
- Public `GET /api/v1/brand` and `GET /api/v1/brand/images/{kind}` serve it to
  the sign-in page and the console.
- Every value is checked at startup: https-only links, a bare email address,
  `#rrggbb`, names without markup; images at most 512 KiB, identified by
  content (PNG, JPEG, WebP, ICO, SVG), SVG rebuilt from drawing elements and
  refused when it carries script, event handlers or external references. An
  invalid brand stops the API from starting.

### Added: platform console Configuration page and version check switch

- Settings > Configuration lists every operator setting with where it is
  managed (this console, applied at once, or the server, restart needed),
  where its value comes from (console, server, default), who last changed a
  console setting, and the page that changes it. Secrets show only whether
  they are set. `GET /api/v1/admin/configuration`, any admin role.
- System > Software updates can turn the daily version check on and off
  without a restart (super admin, step-up, audited `version_check.switched`).
  `VERSION_CHECK_ENABLED=false` stays a ceiling: the console cannot turn the
  check on.

### Added: the platform console image is released and runs in the all-in-one image

- Every release builds, smoke-tests, guards (size, non-root, no setuid, no fixable HIGH/CRITICAL OS advisory), signs (keyless cosign), attests (SLSA provenance, SPDX SBOM) and publishes `ghcr.io/openctemio/openctem-console` for amd64 and arm64, like every other image.
- The all-in-one image (`ghcr.io/openctemio/openctem`) starts the console on loopback port 3001 with the API's console listener on 127.0.0.1:8081, and its gateway serves the console's site on port 8443 (`OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=port`, private client networks only; `off` runs no console). With `GATEWAY=off` the console listens on port 3001 for your own proxy.
- **Upgrade note (all-in-one):** publish port 8443 to reach the console (`-p 8443:8443`), or set `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_SITE=host` with `OPENCTEM_ADMIN_HOST`. The main site no longer serves the console.

### Added: security keys in the platform console screens

- Console sign-in offers "Use security key or passkey" first when the administrator has one, with the authenticator app (when still allowed) and a one-time recovery code as fallbacks.
- The step-up dialog confirms protected actions with a key and retries the action inside the five-minute window; forms that ask for an authenticator code accept an empty code from an administrator with a key.
- New page Security > My security keys: add, rename and remove keys, and generate recovery codes (shown once, copy or download, acknowledged before the dialog closes).
- System > Admin sign-in gets the "Require security keys" switch; under the policy an administrator who still has to enroll sees only the security-keys page until they comply.

### Added: CAPTCHA, deployment region, storage quota, alert webhook and AI provider in the platform console

- Settings > CAPTCHA: the Turnstile site key and secret, set without a restart, with a "check the secret key" button. The secret is encrypted and never shown again; one CAPTCHA serves registration, request access and the tenant and console sign-ins.
- Settings > Configuration: the deployment region can be set once, while no organization exists, and never changes afterwards.
- Settings > Limits: the default storage quota per organization. New limit key `storage_mb` sets one organization's own quota on its Limits tab.
- Settings > Alerts: an HTTPS webhook that receives the administrator alerts (low disk, stale backups, expiring certificates, setting changes), optionally signed (`X-OpenCTEM-Signature`), with a "send a test alert" button.
- Settings > AI provider: the platform AI provider, model and key, off by default, with a "test the key" button.
- Changing the CAPTCHA, the region, the alert webhook or the AI provider needs a super admin, a fresh confirmation and a reason; it writes a critical admin audit row (never a secret) and tells every administrator.

### Added: browse accounts by state and manage the content catalog in the platform console

- Customers > Users lists every account newest first, with state tabs and counts (all, active, not verified, locked, blocked, no MFA, platform admins), an optional search and pagination. Operations admins and super admins only; the list carries no names and no organization data, and every list view is written to the admin audit log (`platform_user.list`). `GET /api/v1/admin/platform-users` takes an optional `state` and no longer requires `q`.
- Scanning > Content catalog: the instance catalog's trust state (the trust roots stay on the server and are shown read-only), its packages and versions, and the guarded actions: import a signed bundle, publish an instance package, revoke a version (super admin, reason, step-up, audited). New read routes `GET /api/v1/admin/content-catalog/packages` and `/packages/{package_id}/versions` list the instance catalog only, never an organization's private package or installation.

### Added: console Content page for the content catalog

- Settings > Content catalog (`/settings/content`, `content:read`) lists the imported signed packages with type,
  search and installed filters, and opens a package to show its versions, permissions, license, dependencies,
  revocation, signatures and provenance.
- Members with `content:install` install, update (with what the new version asks for beyond the installed one
  highlighted), roll back, pin and uninstall packages, and approve, reject or cancel requests; the approval
  option (`settings:write`) shows a pending switch-off and its time.
- A banner warns when the signed index has expired or the revocation list is stale.

### Added: content catalog with offline import, installs, approval and revocation

- New tables (migration 002571) and permissions `content:read` and `content:install` (owners and administrators get
  both, members and viewers `content:read`).
- `POST /api/v1/admin/content-catalog/import` (super admin, reason and console authenticator code, audited)
  verifies a signed offline bundle and stores it in one transaction, with rollback protection on the key set,
  index and revocation list (a list with the same sequence must have the same bytes).
- `/api/v1/content`: browse the catalog, install, update, pin, roll back and uninstall packages per organization,
  with an optional approval step (a second member approves), an audit row per action, dependency, compatibility
  and license checks, and revocation that marks installations revoked.
- Approving a request and carrying it out commit in one transaction. Switching the approval option off takes
  effect 24 hours later and notifies the owners and administrators; switching it on is immediate.
- **Upgrade note:** imports are refused until a catalog root is configured (`CONTENT_TRUST_ROOT_KEY_IDS`) or
  pinned in a release. Setting `CONTENT_TRUST_ROOT_KEY_IDS` or `CONTENT_SIGSTORE_TRUSTED_ROOT` writes a
  high-severity admin audit row at startup.

### Added: first-party content packages and the bundle generator

- `cmd/content-bundle` creates the catalog keys (`keygen`, `keyset`) and builds the signed first-party bundle
  (`build`) from the sast-rules release (its Sigstore signature reused as the publisher signature), the sensor
  products of `versions.yaml` (image digests resolved at build time) and the program and vulnerability feed key
  sets (RFC-099 §6).
- Describing the sources as packages changes nothing in how rules, images and feeds are delivered.

### Added: content pack store for organization uploads (RFC-061 K2)

- `/api/v1/content-packs`: upload, list, get, download and revoke immutable packs of templates, rules and wordlists, plus the organization's content-signing public key.
  - Permissions: `scans:content:read` and `scans:content:write` (owner and admin, migration 001384).
  - Uploads and revocations need a recent sign-in.
- **Ingest:**
  - safe in-memory unpacking: no links or devices, path and size limits;
  - a canonical tar whose SHA-256 is the digest;
  - lint and tier classification per kind (nuclei templates, semgrep rules, wordlists, namespaced kinds);
  - a credential scan that blocks the pack until acknowledged;
  - a DSSE signature with the organization's content key.
- **Signing key:** new optional `APP_CONTENT_SIGNING_KEY`. When unset, the key is derived from `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` under its own label.
- **Storage:** archives are stored once per organization and digest, never shared between organizations, and re-checked against the digest whenever they are read.
- Docs: `docs/architecture/content-packs.md`.

### Added: content package format (`openctem.io/package/v1`)

- RFC-099 defines one package format for rules, templates, wordlists, profiles, report templates, playbooks,
  policy packs, tool adapters, sensor products and feeds: a manifest (`package.yaml`) beside an artifact addressed
  by its SHA-256 digest, with permissions, licence (including whether a service may use it), dependencies,
  compatibility ranges and provenance.
- The JSON schema ships in `api/pkg/contentpkg/schema/package.v1.schema.json`; `pkg/contentpkg` parses and
  validates manifests (strict decoding, no YAML anchors or custom tags, bounded size, reserved namespaces).
- No behaviour change yet: signatures, the catalog and the console follow.

### Added: private content packages for an organization and for the instance

- An organization publishes rules, templates and wordlists to itself only (`content:publish`, a recent sign-in;
  namespace = the organization's slug): the artifact becomes one of its content packs, linted, and the statement
  is signed with its content key. Platform super administrators publish to every organization of the instance.
- Revoking a private version revokes every installation of it. Migration 002886 adds the pack links and the
  `content:publish` permission (owners and administrators).

### Added: CVE corpus tables for inventory matching

- `cve_records` and `vulnerability_affected` (RFC-066 §5.3): for each CVE with a vulnerable product statement, one row per affected range of a global catalog product (exact version or bounds, edition, target, "running on" condition, source). Platform-wide, no tenant data, written only by the vulnerability bundle importer; a trigger refuses ranges that name a tenant-private product.
- Migration 001617. Nothing writes the tables yet: the importer of signed vulnerability bundles comes next.

### Added: the dashboard loads with one request

- `GET /dashboard/overview` returns the CTEM dashboard's reads in one response,
  each part keyed by its endpoint's URL and answered through that endpoint's own
  permission, module and data-scope checks. The dashboard sends one request
  instead of twelve.

### Added: a one-time DAST identity repair

- `refingerprint -dast-repair [-fold-dast-rules r1,r2] [-apply]` folds DAST findings that are one issue under the current recipe. Dry run by default; the earliest-created finding survives with its triage; the others become audited tombstones; idempotent.

### Added: a tool a sensor declares joins the organization's tool catalog

- A tool a sensor reports in its manifest with a valid tool contract (RFC-055) is no longer dropped as `unknown-tool` when the catalog has no row for it: the organization's catalog gets a row projected from the tool's descriptor (display name, description, capabilities, target types, settings schema, version), and the tool can be enabled, configured per sensor and scanned with like any catalog tool. A newer version refreshes the row. RFC-092.
- A declared tool never takes a platform tool's name, never overwrites a member's own tool, is limited to 128 per organization and is edited only through its sensor (the API refuses editing or deleting it; deactivating it still works). Platform sensors declare nothing. Its tier, trust, grant and scope rules are unchanged: an operator-installed tool still runs only as T2.

### Added: Dependabot keeps the release images' base images current

- A weekly grouped Dependabot update covers the `FROM` images of every
  release image (`api/Dockerfile*`, `web/Dockerfile`,
  `deploy/allinone/Dockerfile`, `api/deploy/gateway/Dockerfile`): Go, Alpine,
  node, distroless and Postgres patch and minor releases. Majors stay manual.

### Added: one command prepares a Compose install

- `api/deploy/setup.sh <host name> [--acme you@example.com]` writes `.env` from `.env.example` with freshly generated secrets (database roles, Redis, `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `METRICS_TOKEN`), mode 0600. It never overwrites an existing `.env` and never prints a secret. CI renders the stack from it.
- `OPENCTEM_VERSION` is optional: the compose file defaults to the release it ships with (kept in step by `sync-versions.sh`).

### Added: a renamed directory computer stays the same asset

- New strong, single-valued identifier kind `directory_object_id`: the Active Directory objectGUID of a computer, read from the `ad_object_guid` property the directory collector sends (also `object_guid`, `directory_object_id`). A computer renamed or moved in the directory matches its existing asset instead of becoming a second one; two different objectGUIDs on one name veto a match like other single-valued kinds.
- Migration 002083 widens the `asset_identifiers` kind and strong CHECK constraints. The vCenter instance UUID was already the `cloud_id` identifier.
- Matching stays inside the tenant: the same objectGUID in another organization is a different asset.

### Added: passive lookalike-domain monitoring

- Attack surface › Lookalikes watches the organization's root domains (a
  permanent domain scope entry or a verified domain) for registered
  lookalikes: typos, keyboard neighbours, hyphens, bit flips, look-alike
  characters (incl. IDN) and other TLDs, tunable per domain (en, vi).
  RFC-083.
- Checks are passive only: DNS through the platform resolver and Certificate
  Transparency (crt.sh); no lookalike host is contacted. Registered names are
  re-checked daily, the rest weekly.
- A registered lookalike is a `lookalike_domain` exposure (medium with mail
  servers, or addresses and a certificate) announced like other EASM
  exposures, and triaged as ours or benign, not a threat, or taken down. One
  that stops resolving is resolved.
- `/api/v1/easm/lookalikes/watches` (scope permissions, audited).
- The organization can turn the crt.sh queries for lookalikes off on the
  monitoring card (`lookalike_ct_enabled`, on by default); DNS checks continue.

### Added: AS number and organization seeds for attack surface discovery

- Scoping › Scope › Networks: add the organization's AS numbers and
  organization names (`/api/v1/easm/network-seeds`, scope permissions,
  audited, at most 50). RFC-082.
- An AS seed is looked up in public routing data (RIPEstat, through the SSRF
  guard): its holder and the prefixes it announces, each checked against the
  platform guardrails and offered as a CIDR scope entry through the normal
  scope flow. An organization seed lists the AS numbers registered to it.
  Cloud and CDN networks offer no prefixes. A seed never authorizes a scan.
- The review queue offers the range around an address in a seeded network.
- Seeds are refreshed weekly; a refresh can be requested once per 15 minutes.
- The organization can turn the RIPEstat lookups off on the monitoring card
  (`network_lookups_enabled` on `/api/v1/easm/settings`, on by default).

### Added: attack surface suggestion cards

- New `GET /api/v1/easm/suggestions`, read only and narrowed to the caller's
  data scope. It returns the scope decisions that still need a person, one
  card each:
  - `addresses_behind_names`: the addresses your in-scope names resolve to,
    as one grouped suggestion instead of a review row per address. Shared,
    CDN and other organizations' addresses are listed apart with the reason
    and are never offered. An address whose network is unknown is counted
    as such and never presented as safe.
  - `confirmed_out_of_scope`: assets a person confirmed that no scope entry
    covers.
- Accepting a card is an ordinary bulk add of exact scope entries. Nothing
  is ever added automatically.

### Added: what changed on the attack surface, and a weekly digest

- `GET /api/v1/easm/changes` lists typed changes of the external attack
  surface: new and removed hosts, opened and closed ports, new and expiring
  certificates, DNS changes and dangling records, technology changes and new
  exposures, with counts per kind, narrowed to the caller's data scope
  (RFC-080).
- Attack surface › Changes shows them by kind and window (en, vi).
- Each organization gets a weekly digest of those changes (in-app for owners
  and administrators, and the `attack_surface_digest` notification event,
  added to every channel that already receives `new_exposure`). It is on by
  default, sent once per week on the chosen weekday at 08:00 UTC, silent for a
  week without changes, and switched off or moved on the monitoring card
  (`weekly_digest_enabled`, `digest_weekday` on `/api/v1/easm/settings`).

### Added: web evidence and optional screenshots of web assets

- Sensors can attach captures to a web asset (final URL, status, title,
  server, the first 4 KiB of the response with secrets masked, and an optional
  screenshot) in the reserved `web_evidence` asset property; the asset page
  shows them in a Web evidence card (en, vi). RFC-081.
- Screenshots are kept only when the organization turns on "Screenshots of
  web assets" (`web_screenshots_enabled` on `/api/v1/easm/settings`, off by
  default), re-encoded to PNG within 1 MiB and 1920x2400 px, stored in the
  organization's file storage and deleted after 30 days.
- `GET /api/v1/assets/{id}/web-evidence` and
  `GET /api/v1/assets/{id}/web-evidence/{evidence_id}/screenshot`
  (`assets:read`, the asset's data scope; the image is served sandboxed).

### Added: one environment variable registry; misspelled or unparseable variables stop startup

- `internal/config/env_registry.yaml` lists every environment variable the API, its tools, the web console, the gateway, the Compose stack and the all-in-one image read: type, default, required, secret, description. A test keeps it equal to what the code reads, including literal defaults.
- `api/.env.example` and the new `api/docs/configuration/environment-variables.md` are generated from it (`make env-docs`; a test fails when they are stale). `.env.example` now lists only what a development checkout sets (64 lines instead of about 490); everything else keeps its default.
- **Behaviour change:** startup refuses a variable under an API prefix (`SMTP_`, `AUTH_`, `SENSOR_`, ...) that is not registered but is within three edits of a registered name, with a "did you mean" hint (for example `SMTP_PASWORD`). Other unregistered names under those prefixes are logged as warnings. Kubernetes service-link variables are ignored.
- **Behaviour change:** a set API variable whose value does not parse as its type (`SERVER_PORT=abc`, `SENSOR_KEY_TTL=30d`, `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=yes`) now stops startup instead of silently using the default. Messages name variables, never values.
- `server -check-config` also lists which API variables are set (names only) and the warnings.

### Added: tools push typed evidence (CTIS 1.6 evidence_items); imports keep the HTTP proof

- Ingest reads `finding.evidence_items` from any tool, the third-party tier included: `http_exchange`, `raw_text`, `command_output`, `file_excerpt`, `screenshot`, `curl`, and any other kind, kept as text. They are capped and masked by the platform like the nuclei properties before them, whatever the tool marked.
- The API pins ctis main: a nuclei, SARIF (`webRequest`/`webResponse`), HAR or ZAP file imported through `POST /api/v1/findings/import` now keeps each finding's request, response and reproduction command as evidence.
- nuclei masks `Authorization` and `Cookie` itself (`***`); those values stay masked and are not revealable.

### Added: console views for external members, trusted organizations and personal accounts

- **Organization switcher:**
  - marks organizations where you are an external member and says when your access there ends;
  - disables an organization you cannot open, with the reason;
  - offers a search above seven organizations.
  - `GET /users/me/tenants` returns `kind`, `access_expires_at` and `blocked_reason` for each membership.
- **Members:**
  - Internal / External filter (`?kind=`);
  - badges: External, Personal, Unmanaged, Lapsed domain, SSO exception, end of access;
  - "Change end of access" for external members.
- **Invitations:** an end of access for people outside the organization, and a warning when the address looks like an existing member's.
- **Settings › Trusted organizations:** request, approve, change and end trusts with partner organizations.
- **Settings › Authentication:**
  - the personal-accounts policy;
  - while SSO is enforced, the SSO exception list.
- **Platform administrator console:** each verified SSO domain of an organization shows and changes how SSO treats newcomers (role, or not admitted).

### Added: chunked program feed import with a resumable checkpoint

- The public program feed importer reads bundle format v2 (signed pointer, signed manifests, content-addressed chunks) through the sdk-go transfer layer when the source offers it: retries with back-off, Range resume, mirror fall-back, a verified chunk cache, and each chunk applied in its own transaction with a durable checkpoint, so a crash or a dropped connection resumes at the next chunk. The whole-bundle (v1) reader stays the fallback for this release. Every existing check is kept (pinned root, key-set version, sequence newer than applied, delta base, expiry, caps, per-record validation, local-only bundles only through the local path).
- New table `feed_checkpoints` (migration `feed_checkpoints`), platform-wide with no tenant data, backfilled from the applied sequences of `program_feed_state`.
- New optional settings: `PROGRAMFEED_URL`, `PROGRAMFEED_MIRRORS` (https only) and `FEED_CACHE_DIR`.
- The API now requires `github.com/openctemio/sdk-go`. **Dev note:** a local `sdk-go` checkout mounted at `/app/sdk-go` is used only when it builds with the API (sdk-go `main`); otherwise the go.mod pin is used.

### Added: every status change on a finding's timeline records the lifecycle version

- `finding_activities.lifecycle_version` (also in the entry's `changes` as `lifecycle_version`) is set on every timeline entry that records a status change, whatever wrote it: a person's move, a platform writer, or the transition timeline trigger. Today it is `platform:1`. A tenant lifecycle scheme will record its own version, so an audit can tell which rules applied when a finding moved.
- Older entries stay empty: they were decided before versions were recorded.
- Migration `002540_finding_activity_lifecycle_version` adds a nullable column (a catalog change) and a BEFORE INSERT trigger.

### Added: approvers are told about finding false-positive and accepted-risk requests, with reminders

- A new request (from a person or an AI triage proposal) notifies the members
  who may decide it, in-app (notification type `finding_approval`) and by
  email: owners, admins and roles holding `findings:approve`, whose data scope
  holds the finding. The requester is never notified as an approver, and an
  approver outside the finding's data scope is not told.
- The email carries the finding title, the requested status and the dates,
  never the justification; its link opens the approvals inbox (sign-in
  required).
- `POST /api/v1/approvals/{id}/remind` (`findings:write`, the finding in the
  caller's data scope) reminds the same approvers, at most once an hour per
  request (409 otherwise), audited as `finding_approval.reminded`.
- Migration `002600` (`finding_approval_reminded_at`): a nullable column.
- VEX-created requests (batch, per scan report) are not notified one by one
  yet.

### Added: where and when a finding was seen, in the finding drawer

- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}` returns `provenance`: the branches the finding was seen on with their first and last commit and status, and, for a caller holding `scans:ci:read`, the CI pipelines that reported it (the newest five and the first one, with the pipeline link and merge request). Run actors and tokens are never included.
- The finding drawer has a Provenance section: first seen (branch, commit, pipeline, merge request), last seen, every branch with its commits (linked to the repository when its address is known) and the recent pipelines.

### Added: cross-rule correlation of DAST findings

- Two rules that report one issue on the same injection point (a generic detection and a CVE template; or one CVE from two templates) become one finding: the CVE finding is the primary, the other its reversible duplicate. The injection point keeps scheme, host, port, path, method and parameter names; a template's out-of-band payload is removed from the path only when the detection's own response echoed it and its host is a known out-of-band domain.
- Correlation only reduces noise: broad or missing CWEs, two different CVEs, other assets or CWEs never merge; less certain pairs are "possibly related" suggestions. The duplicate is re-derived every scan and released (as a new finding) when its primary was not seen or was triaged; triage never propagates.
- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}/detections`, `POST /api/v1/findings/{id}/correlation/release` and `/approve`, a per-organization switch (`/settings/finding-correlation`), and `refingerprint -correlate` for existing findings.

### Added: dependency findings say whether the package is direct and the chain that brings it in

- A dependency finding keeps the scanner's `is_direct` and `dependency_path` (CTIS; trivy through the CI runner or an uploaded trivy report): at most 32 package ids, replaced on each sighting.
- The finding detail returns them on `component` as `dependency_type` (`direct` or `transitive`) and `dependency_path`, with `manifest_line`, the package's line in the lock file.
- ctis is updated to the version whose trivy importer reports them.

### Added: the finding drawer says which dependency brings a vulnerable package in

- The Fix card of a dependency finding reads "Direct dependency" or "Transitive via express@4.17.1 → …" (long chains keep both ends; the full chain is in the tooltip).
- The lock file shows the package's line and links to it in the repository at the scanned commit when the repository URL is known.

### Added: evidence by finding type, j/k navigation and shareable links in the finding drawer

- SAST findings show their data flow in the drawer: numbered source → steps → sink with file, line and code (six steps, the rest on the full page), and "Open the code" at the reported commit in GitLab, GitHub, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps.
- Secret findings show the masked value, the kind, whether the scanner verified it and where it is; the value itself is never shown (revealing stays on the full page, permission-gated and audited).
- DAST and EASM findings show the scanner's HTTP evidence (masked) in the drawer.
- `j` / `k` open the next / previous finding of the list while the drawer is open, and the open finding is kept in the address (`#finding=<id>`), so the link can be shared and a reload reopens it.

### Added: import results exported by other tools

- `POST /api/v1/findings/import` and the Findings > Import results dialog take a file exported by another tool (Nessus, Qualys with its KnowledgeBase, SARIF, trivy, grype, semgrep, gitleaks, nuclei, ZAP, vuls, CycloneDX, SPDX, OSV scanner results, CSAF, OpenVEX, DefectDojo Generic Findings) or a ZIP of them. The format is detected from the content; a preview parses and counts without writing, with problems and their line numbers and the source fields not recognized.
- Every committed file is recorded in `finding_imports` (uploader, format, a hash of the file name, counts; migration 001142). Its id is the `scan_id` of the findings it wrote and the new `assets.import_id` of the assets it wrote, and the response and audit records return it.
- The import runs with the uploader's rights: findings land only on assets in their data scope, and an import never auto-resolves anything.
- VEX documents are matched against the organization's findings by vulnerability id and package; a statement about components inside a product applies only to that product's findings. Statements are stored on the matched findings; a `not_affected` statement closes open, non-human findings only under `INGEST_VEX=enforce` and for an uploader with `findings:approve`.

### Added: vulnerability intelligence with sources and dates in the finding drawer

- Ingest keeps the scanner advisory's references (http(s) only, at most 25), published and modified dates and the primary CVSS source on the finding, since a report never writes the shared CVE catalog.
- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}` returns `intel`: those facts plus the date of the EPSS score and the CISA KEV date added (and ransomware use) for the finding's CVE.
- The finding drawer has an Intelligence section: every CVSS score with its version, vector and source, a note when the sources disagree, the CWE, KEV status with its dates, EPSS with its percentile and date, published and updated dates, the identifiers (CVE, GHSA, OSV) linked to their authority, and the references with advisory databases and fix commits first.

### Added: finding lifecycle definitions API (sub-statuses and lifecycle schemes)

- New routes `/api/v1/lifecycle-sub-statuses` and `/api/v1/lifecycles` (RFC-110). An organization defines
  sub-statuses (labels bound to one canonical status and, under a closed status, one closure reason) and
  lifecycle schemes with versions: draft (edited with `If-Match`), validate, publish, roll back. A scheme
  can only add constraints to the platform's status rules; nothing evaluates it yet.
- New permission `findings:lifecycles:write`, granted to owners and administrators (migration
  `002776_finding_lifecycles_permission`). Reading needs `findings:read`. Publishing needs a recent sign-in
  (step-up) and is audited.
- New plan limits `lifecycle_sub_statuses` (Free: 3) and `lifecycle_schemes` (Free: 0, Pro: 1).

### Added: groundwork for organization finding lifecycles (sub-statuses)

- New tables `lifecycle_sub_statuses`, `lifecycle_schemes` and `lifecycle_scheme_versions`, and a nullable
  `findings.sub_status_id` (RFC-110). A sub-status is an organization's label bound for ever to one
  canonical status (and, under a closed status, to one closure reason); the database refuses a sub-status of
  another tenant or another status, and any status change that does not name a new sub-status falls back
  to the default label. Nothing uses them yet: no behaviour changes.
- Migrations `002767_lifecycle_catalog`, `002768_findings_sub_status_fk` (foreign key `NOT VALID`),
  `002769_findings_sub_status_fk_validate` and `002770_findings_sub_status_index` (built concurrently). Every
  existing finding has no sub-status, so the validation and the index are quick; no long locks.

### Added: findings show their sub-status, and the status menu offers the lifecycle's moves

- The findings list, the drawer and the finding page show the organization's sub-status next to the
  status.
- The status menu lists the moves the organization's lifecycle allows, including moves onto a
  sub-status, with what each needs; a move that needs a longer note or fields (ticket link, fix reference,
  change ID, target version, due date, compensating control) asks for them before it is sent.
- A bulk status change reports up front the findings whose move needs fields or a longer note.

### Added: finding status moves follow the organization's published lifecycle

- Every status path (`PATCH /findings/{id}/status`, bulk status, the fix-applied, verify and reject
  actions, remediation group and campaign resolves, ticket webhooks, approval requests) is also decided by
  the organization's published lifecycle (RFC-110). It can only narrow the platform's decision: a longer
  note, required fields, a required permission, keeping automation or ticket sync off a move. It never
  lets a move past `findings:verify`, the evidence rules, the fix-claim rules or four-eyes approval.
- `PATCH /findings/{id}/status` takes `sub_status_id` and `fields`; the finding resource carries
  `sub_status_id`; `GET /findings/{id}/transitions` and the bulk preview list sub-status moves and what each
  needs. A sub-status changes only through these moves, each on the timeline with the lifecycle version
  that decided it. Organizations without a published lifecycle see no change.

### Added: Settings → Findings → Finding lifecycle in the web console

- A new Findings group in Settings holds Finding lifecycle, Finding approvals and Vulnerability matching.
- Finding lifecycle manages the organization's sub-statuses (a lane per status: add, rename, colour,
  reorder, archive, reactivate) and its lifecycles: edit the draft's moves and their requirements, check
  it against the validator, publish it (a recent sign-in is asked for) and roll back to an earlier version.
- Read-only for members with `findings:read`; changing needs `findings:lifecycles:write`. Plan limits on
  sub-statuses and lifecycles are shown, and adding stops at the limit.

### Added: a pentest finding's retest history shows the testers' retests

- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}/retests` now lists, for a pentest finding, the
  retests testers recorded by hand (`kind: manual`, with `manual_result`,
  `notes` and `tested_by`) next to automated retests (`kind: automated`),
  newest first: one history per finding. The finding page shows them.
- For a pentest finding the history follows the campaign's rule: only
  campaign members and admins see it; anyone else gets 404, as on every other
  pentest surface.

### Added: the nearest fixed version and an upgrade plan for dependency findings

- Ingest keeps the scanner's fixed versions on each finding (`metadata.fixed_versions`; trivy's comma-separated list is split, bounded to 20 entries). Findings from CI and sensor reports, which do not write the shared CVE catalog, now get a nearest fix.
- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}`: `component.fixed_in` is the nearest fix for the installed version (same major line first), `component.fixed_in_major` flags a breaking upgrade, `component.fixed_versions` lists every release line's fix, and `component.manifest_file` falls back to the finding's file. New `package_fix`: the version that fixes the most open findings of the same package version on the same asset, which ones it fixes and which stay open, and the lowest version that fixes all of them when the installed line no longer gets fixes.
- The Fix card in the finding drawer and page reads "Upgrade Django 4.2.20 → 4.2.26" instead of listing every release line, flags a major upgrade, and says "Upgrading Django to 4.2.30 fixes 22 of 30 open findings of this package on this asset" with the list.

### Added: findings keep what their source knew (CTIS 1.4)

- Findings store the CTIS 1.4 interoperability members per sighting: the native identity (plugin ID / QID / rule, native severity and status, detection type, credentialed flag), every score with its system, version, source and date (CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 together, VPR and other vendor scores, EPSS, SSVC), typed vulnerability ids, the source lifecycle, solution metadata, the latest VEX statement, unmapped source fields and the normalized location (migration 001117). The finding detail returns them as `source_data`.
- A report that sends its CVE only in `vulnerability.ids`, or its check id only in `native.vuln_id`, is keyed like one that sends `cve_id` / `rule_id`; reports that already set those keep their fingerprints.
- Asset `identity_hints` (FQDN, NetBIOS name, MACs, cloud resource id) count in asset matching like the same values under their usual property names.

### Added: one transition engine for finding status changes, and the allowed moves of a finding

- Every status change made by a person or a delegated actor is decided by one engine. That covers the status endpoint, bulk status, the fix-applied / verify / reject-fix actions and their by-filter variants, approval requests and decisions, remediation group and campaign resolves, workflow `update_status`, and the Jira and GitHub webhooks. Approvals still need a second person, as before.
- `GET /api/v1/findings/{id}/transitions` lists every move from the finding's status for the caller: allowed or not, how (direct, an approval request, the duplicate picker), the inputs it needs, and reason codes when blocked.
- `POST /api/v1/findings/transitions/preview` (`finding_ids`, at most 100, and `to`) is a dry run with a decision per finding.
- Both need `findings:read`, and both are tenant- and data-scoped: out-of-scope findings are 404 on the GET and `not_found` in the dry run.
- The MCP tool `list_finding_transitions` returns the same answer.
- A false-positive or accepted-risk request is refused (404) for a finding outside the caller's data scope.
- Pentest findings are refused on the verify and reject-fix actions too, as on every other status route. The pentest module owns their moves.

### Added: GitHub App installations for CI checks and pull request comments

- A deployment can register the OpenCTEM GitHub App (`GITHUB_APP_ID`,
  `GITHUB_APP_SLUG`, `GITHUB_APP_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_CLIENT_SECRET`,
  `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE`, `GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; steps in
  `docs/how-to/github-app.md`). Permissions: checks and pull requests write,
  metadata read.
- An organization binds its installation (`GET /api/v1/ci/scm-apps`,
  `POST /api/v1/ci/scm-apps/github/install-url`,
  `POST /api/v1/ci/scm-apps/github/installations`,
  `DELETE /api/v1/ci/scm-apps/installations/{id}`; `scans:ci:write` to change).
  Binding needs the install state the console issued to the person for that
  organization (15 minutes) and the person's own GitHub authorization reaching
  the installation; one installation belongs to one organization. Audited
  (`scm_app.installed`, `scm_app.removed`).
- `POST /api/v1/hooks/github-app` takes installation events,
  verified with the app's webhook secret before anything is read: a deleted or
  suspended installation stops being used at once (`scm_app.status_changed`).
- Posting the check and comments follows in the next change (RFC-077 phase C).

### Added: GitHub repository rename, transfer and archive events keep assets and CI pipelines in step

- The GitHub App webhook now handles `repository` events. `renamed` and `transferred` rename the repository's asset and CI pipelines, found by GitHub's immutable repository id inside the organization the installation is bound to (a name another asset holds is left alone). `archived` flags the repository's pipelines as archived (no stale alerts, findings not marked not observed) and `unarchived` revives them. CI trust configurations are never edited by a webhook. Subscribe the app to the **Repository** event (new apps from the manifest in the how-to already do). Migration adds `ci_pipelines.repository_archived_at`.

### Added: a step-by-step GitLab CI/CD guide

- `docs/how-to/gitlab-ci.md`: trusting a GitLab project, the two CI/CD
  variables, the template or a single job, enforcing the gate on merge
  requests, the first default-branch run, self-managed GitLab, security notes
  and troubleshooting. No API key is stored in GitLab.

### Added: idle Free workspaces

- A Free organization that nobody signs in to is reminded at 60 days (email to its owners and admins), becomes read-only at 90 days (changes refused with 403 `WORKSPACE_READ_ONLY`, reads keep working), gets a final warning at 113 days and is due for deletion at 120 days, when the platform administrators are alerted. Nothing is deleted automatically. A sign-in by any member undoes it at once. Every step is audited.
- Platform administrators see the stage at `GET /api/v1/admin/tenants/{tenantId}/idle` and can exempt an organization with a reason (`PUT .../idle/exemption`, ops_admin+).
- Pro, Enterprise and organizations without a plan are never affected. Migration 001347 (new, empty table).

### Added: release images pass a size, non-root and OS-advisory gate before they are pushed

- `.github/scripts/image-guard.sh` runs on every image of a release (each
  architecture, before the push) and on the merge queue's image builds: a
  per-image size budget, a non-root user, no setuid/setgid file, and no
  fixable HIGH/CRITICAL advisory in OS packages (trivy). Advisories in
  application dependencies are listed as warnings.

### Added: ingest accepts CTIS 1.5 and binds sensor reports to their capability

- **CTIS 1.5.** The API reads CTIS 1.5 reports (ctis `main`): `metadata.capability`, `asset.technologies`, `relationships` and `finding.attack`. This is the receiver-first step, so sensors can send them later. Reports of 1.0 to 1.4 are unchanged.
- **Tool contracts.** A tool contract in the sensor manifest keeps:
  - `implements`, the capability references of the tool's descriptor (`scan.ports@1`), matched exactly against the ctis taxonomy;
  - `batch`;
  - `origin` (`builtin` or `adapter`).
- **Capability of a command-bound report.** The platform derives it from the command's tool: its catalog stages, plus the capabilities it declares in its sensor's manifest (tenant-scoped).
  - The sensor's `metadata.capability` is kept only when it names one of those candidates.
  - A report that is not bound to a command has no capability.
- **Port-closure reconciliation** (a port missing from the next scan is closed) now applies to any report bound to `scan.ports`, not only to tools on a name list.
- **Finding source by capability.** The detection technique of a bound report (SAST, secret, SCA, container, IaC, DAST, EASM, VA, CSPM) comes from its capability, so a third-party tool needs no entry in the tool-name table. Unbound reports keep the name rules. A report bound to `secrets.code` is masked as a secret scan whatever its tool is called.
- **Required output.** A report that misses the required output of its capability is logged and counted (`capability_contract_warned`) and applied as before. This is warn first, per decision TC13 of RFC-055.

### Added: internal entitlements API for a hosted service's control plane (off by default)

- A separate listener (`INTERNAL_API_ADDR`, empty by default) lets a hosted service's control plane set per-organization limits and module denies, the self-service default limits, the idle policy, provision organizations, and read aggregate usage counts. See `docs/architecture/limits.md`, "Internal entitlements API".
- Trust: mTLS (TLS 1.3, client certificate from `INTERNAL_API_CLIENT_CA` required) plus a short-lived (at most 5 minutes), single-use, Ed25519-signed token per request with scopes `limits:write`, `orgs:provision` or `usage:read`. Every write is audited as actor `control-plane`. No endpoint returns organization content.
- Self-hosted installs need nothing: with the listener off, nothing changes and limits written by a control plane are ignored.
- **Upgrade note:** only for a hosted service: set every `INTERNAL_API_` variable (the API refuses to start when the address is set and a file is missing).

### Added: find expired and expiring certificates and domains in the inventory

- `GET /api/v1/assets` takes `expires_before` and `expires_after` (RFC 3339
  or YYYY-MM-DD). They match the asset's expiry: a certificate's
  `not_after` or a domain's `expires_at`. A malformed or missing expiry
  never matches.
- The registry marks those keys with the new property format `expiry`, so a
  new expiry key needs no code. The web reads the format instead of a key
  list.
- The inventory's Views menu has "Expired" and "Expiring in 30 days" on the
  list of every type and on a typed list with an expiry (certificates,
  domains).

### Added: asset counts on the inventory lenses, with type chips

- `GET /api/v1/assets/stats` returns `by_type_sub_type` (keyed `type` or `type/sub_type`, data-scoped like every other count), so the web places each asset in its registry lens.
- The inventory's lens bar shows each lens's count, hides lenses with no asset, adds **Other** for assets outside every lens (unclassified), and with a lens picked lists its asset types with counts as multi-select chips (`?types=`). The type filter in the side panel is removed: the bar is the one place to filter by type; saved views and links with `?types=` keep working.

### Added: filter the asset inventory by lens and by minimum risk

- `GET /api/v1/assets` and `GET /api/v1/assets/stats` take
  `lenses=<lens>,...`, matching the stored lens of each asset, so an alias
  stored under another type's name (a container registry stored as storage)
  is listed with its own lens. An unknown lens is refused with 400.
- The inventory shows the lenses as pills above the list (`/assets?lens=`),
  and the stats strip has a "High risk" metric that filters to a risk score
  of 70 or more (`min_risk_score`). The inventory overview links each lens
  card to its lens, and its high-risk count to that filter.

### Added: inventory triage filters, bulk "mark out of scope" and the undo of a decision

- `GET /assets` filters `scope_status` (`in_scope`, `not_covered`, `excluded`, `internal`), `discovered_by`, `discovery_technique`, `min_confidence`, `max_confidence` and `first_seen_after`; `with_triage=true` adds each row's attribution and the active-scan gate's answer (RFC-054 §15).
- `POST /scope/exclusions/bulk/preview` and `POST /scope/exclusions/bulk`: mark up to 200 names or rules out of scope at once, with a preview of the visible assets each would match; the undo is the existing bulk delete.
- `POST /easm/candidates/decisions` accepts `state: "automatic"`: forget a person's decision (the undo of "Not ours").

### Added: invitation preview, resend limits and revoked invitations kept

- `POST /api/v1/organization/invitations/preview` tells the inviter, before sending, whether the organization's invitation policy allows the address (with a reason code), whether the person is outside the organization or uses a personal address, whether the roles need the inviter's re-authentication and the member's two-factor, whether an end of access is required, and whether they are already a member or invited. It reveals nothing about other organizations.
- The pending invitations list shows whether the invitee is outside the organization, whether two-factor will be required, the end of access, the last send and the number of resends.
- Migration `invitation_lifecycle` adds `revoked_at`, `last_sent_at`, `resend_count`, `invitee_kind` and `privileged` to `tenant_invitations`.

### Added: invitations can add the invitee to teams

- `POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant}/invitations` and `POST /api/v1/organization/invitations/preview` accept `group_ids` (up to 20). The invitee joins those teams when they accept, so they no longer join with no data.
- The inviter can add only teams they may add a member to. A team carrying a privileged role needs the owner, with step-up. An external team needs an end of access. A person outside the organization never gets full data access through a team. A team carrying a role above member makes an outside invitee privileged, so the inviter must step up and the invitee needs two-factor. Teams from another organization are refused (404).
- At acceptance the teams are checked again for the inviter. A team they can no longer add to, or one deleted since, voids the invitation, and nothing is granted.
- Migration `002186` adds `tenant_invitations.group_ids` (empty by default; no operator step).

### Added: teams in the invite dialog, and an acceptance page that says what the invitee gets

- The invite dialog lists the organization's active teams. The inviter can add the invitee to some of them, so the person does not join with no data. A team the inviter cannot add people to is explained before sending.
- The public invitation lookup (`POST /api/v1/invitations/lookup`) returns:
  - the roles with their risk summary;
  - the teams;
  - the end of access;
  - whether the person is outside the organization;
  - whether two-factor authentication will be required, and why.
- The acceptance page shows all of this before the person accepts.
- Declining is offered to everyone, signed in or not. It asks for confirmation and then says that the invitation was declined, instead of redirecting.
- The acceptance page's text is translated (English and Vietnamese).

### Added: Jira status changes follow the published mapping profile

- When a Jira project has a published finding mapping profile, its inbound
  status rules decide what a status change means: Done is a fix claim
  (verification queued), In Progress starts work, and "Won't Do" (or the
  resolution the profile names) opens a pending risk-acceptance or
  false-positive request. A request is made by the linked ticket, never by a
  person, and a person with the approve permission decides it; an
  in-progress finding goes back to confirmed once its request exists (it
  stays in progress when a request is already pending or cannot be made). The issue gets one comment
  saying what was requested or refused. A ticket still never closes a finding.
- A Jira status change of an issue outside the projects configured for
  ticketing moves no finding (the same rule as linking an existing issue).
- Approvals list a ticket's request as "Linked ticket".

### Added: one Jira issue per remediation task

- A person who may change a remediation task creates its Jira issue
  (`POST /api/v1/remediation/tasks/{task_id}/ticket-links`, `remediation:write`)
  in a project configured for ticketing; a task has at most one issue. The
  issue carries the task's title, fix, finding count, deadline and a link back,
  and names no finding.
- The issue follows the task: in progress and done move it, and every move of
  the task posts a progress comment (findings closed, verified, fix claimed,
  in progress, open). A missed push is retried every minute.
- Moving the task's issue to Done in Jira claims the fix of the task's open
  findings; OpenCTEM verifies each of them. Our own moves are not read back.

### Added: the platform learns each tool's time per target

- Every completed scan command is one sample of its tool's time per target
  in its organization (duration × targets worked on at once ÷ targets),
  clamped to the tool's floor and ceiling. The platform keeps a decayed mean
  and p95 per organization and tool (`tool_duration_stats`).
- `toolbudget.Lookup(tenant, tool)` returns the tool's budget with what was
  learned (after 5 samples, the per-target budget follows 1.5 × the learned
  p95, always within the tool's band); the planner and the target pool size
  jobs from it. Failed, canceled and re-queued attempts teach nothing.

### Added: legal page templates and security.txt

- `LEGAL_PAGES_ENABLED=true` serves built-in templates for the Terms of Service (`/terms`), Acceptable Use Policy (`/acceptable-use`), Privacy Policy (`/privacy`), Data Processing Addendum (`/dpa`) and subprocessor list (`/subprocessors`). Contacts default to info@openctem.io, security@openctem.io, https://openctem.io and https://docs.openctem.io (each configurable with `LEGAL_*`); the company legal name, address, governing law and effective date show as marked placeholders until set. Off by default (404).
- `LEGAL_TERMS_URL` / `LEGAL_PRIVACY_URL` link documents hosted elsewhere and are read at runtime; the sign-in and register notices link whichever is configured.
- `/.well-known/security.txt` (RFC 9116) is served with security@openctem.io by default and a rolling one-year `Expires`; `SECURITY_CONTACT` (email or https URL) replaces the contact, `SECURITY_POLICY_URL` adds `Policy`, `SECURITY_TXT_ENABLED=false` turns it off.

### Added: organization license policy and license findings

- `GET/PUT /api/v1/organization/settings/license-policy` (`settings:read` / `settings:write`, audited): allow, review or deny per SPDX license id (optionally WITH an exception) or license category, optionally limited to dependency scopes; a verdict for known licenses no rule matches and one for unknown or missing licenses; an opt-in for review findings.
- Declared licenses are evaluated as SPDX expressions (`MIT OR GPL-3.0-only` passes when MIT is allowed; AND needs every term). The verdict is stored on each package link and re-evaluated on every policy change and every package write (sensor, CI, SBOM import).
- A deny verdict opens a high finding (`source = sca`, type `license`), a review verdict a medium one when opted in, per asset, package and declared licenses; findings the policy no longer flags, or whose package went away, are resolved, and reopen when flagged again.
- Migration `001961_license_policy` adds `asset_software.license_verdict` / `license_rule` and the `license` finding type (constraint added NOT VALID, then validated).

### Added: link an existing Jira issue to a finding

- On a finding, "Link an existing issue" takes an issue key or its URL. The
  issue must be on the organization's Jira site and visible to the
  integration (a URL on another host is refused before any call); a moved
  issue is linked under its current key. Only issues in a project the
  organization configured for ticketing (the default project, a routing
  rule's project or a mapping profile's project) can be linked, so the
  platform never transitions or comments on issues elsewhere that the
  integration's account happens to see. Unlinking leaves the issue alone.
  `GET/POST /api/v1/findings/{id}/ticket-links`,
  `DELETE /api/v1/findings/{id}/ticket-links/{link_id}` (`findings:read` /
  `findings:write`, the finding's data scope), audited as
  `finding.ticket_linked` / `finding.ticket_unlinked`.
- Creating a ticket also records its link.

### Added: the platform keeps each tool's full descriptor from the sensor manifest

- A tool on the tool contract reports its whole `tool.yaml` (canonical JSON) in the sensor manifest. The platform now keeps it in the sensor's manifest version, next to the contract: `tools[].contract.descriptor`. `Manifest.ToolDescriptor(name)` reads it. Planning, the workflow builder and the tools API will read the tool's capabilities, params, batch shape and presentation from it (RFC-055).
- A descriptor that does not qualify is dropped and listed in the manifest's ignored items with the reason `invalid-descriptor`; the contract is kept. A descriptor qualifies when it:
  - hashes to the contract's digest;
  - is a JSON object of the same format and version;
  - is at most 64 KiB;
  - holds no control or bidirectional-override character in any string or key.

### Added: members can ask administrators to approve an AI application

- A member whose AI application is blocked because the organization only admits approved applications can now press "Request access" on the consent page. Administrators get an in-app notification and approve or decline the request in Settings, AI assistants (MCP), Applications; approving adds the application's publisher host to the organization's approved publishers. An owner or administrator can also approve the publisher directly from the consent page and continue connecting.
- The server takes every detail of a request from the stored authorization request; requests are limited to 5 new ones per member per day and 50 waiting per organization. Approving needs `settings:write` and a recent sign-in; requests, approvals and declines are audited (`mcp_access_request.created`, `.approved`, `.denied`).
- New endpoints: `POST /api/v1/oauth/requests/{id}/access-request`, `POST /api/v1/oauth/requests/{id}/allow-publisher`, `GET /api/v1/mcp-access/requests`, `POST /api/v1/mcp-access/requests/{id}/approve`, `POST /api/v1/mcp-access/requests/{id}/deny`. Migration `002906_mcp_access_requests` adds one table.

### Added: organizations register their own AI applications

- Settings, AI access (MCP): owners and administrators register an AI
  application (MCP client) with its exact return addresses and give it the
  client id. Members see it as registered by the organization; no other
  organization can use it; deleting it ends its connections. API
  `/api/v1/mcp-access/clients` (RFC-062).
- Optional dynamic client registration (RFC 7591, `POST /oauth/register`)
  for MCP clients that support neither metadata documents nor a client id:
  off unless `MCP_OAUTH_DCR_ENABLED=true`; such applications are always
  unverified and limited to organizations that allow any application.
- A background job purges ended authorization requests, tokens, grants and
  unused clients.
- **Upgrade note:** the gateway sends `/oauth/register` to the API.
